lessons.title: Functions & Function Notation
lessons.description: Deepen understanding of functions including composition, inverses, and domains.
lessons.formula:
Composition: f(g(x))
Apply g first, then f

Inverse: f⁻¹(x) undoes f(x)
f(f⁻¹(x)) = x

Horizontal Line Test:
If any horizontal line crosses
the graph more than once,
it's NOT one-to-one.
lessons.content:
Function composition applies one function to the result of another: f(g(x)) means plug x into g, then put that result into f. It's like a two-step machine! Order matters: f(g(x)) ≠ g(f(x)) in general.

An inverse function f⁻¹ undoes what f does. If f(3) = 7, then f⁻¹(7) = 3. To find inverses, swap x and y and solve for y. Only one-to-one functions (passing the horizontal line test) have inverses.

Piecewise functions have different rules for different parts of the domain. A step function jumps between constant values. Understanding domain restrictions is crucial — many operations change the valid inputs.
steps: For composition f(g(x)): evaluate g(x) first, then substitute into f
For inverse: replace f(x) with y, swap x and y, solve for y
Check if a function is one-to-one using the horizontal line test
For piecewise functions: identify which piece applies based on x
Always check domain restrictions

examples.title: Finding the Inverse of f(x) = 3x + 2
examples.text: Swap: x = 3y + 2. Solve: x − 2 = 3y. y = (x−2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x−2)/3.

lessons.tip: To check an inverse function, verify that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x AND f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. If both compositions give x, your inverse is correct! This is like a round-trip: go there and back, you should end up where you started.

quiz.q: If f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 5, what is f(g(3))?
What is the inverse of f(x) = x + 7?
quiz.explanation: Swap: x = y + 7. Solve: y = x − 7.

quiz.q: A function is one-to-one if it passes the:
quiz.explanation: The horizontal line test: if any horizontal line crosses the graph more than once, it's not one-to-one.

quiz.q: If f(x) = x², what is the domain restriction for the inverse?
quiz.explanation: x² is not one-to-one over all reals. Restrict to x ≥ 0 (or x ≤ 0) to make it one-to-one.

lessons.title: Quadratic Functions & Complex Numbers
lessons.description: Graph quadratics in vertex form and perform operations with complex numbers!
lessons.formula:
Vertex Form: y = a(x − h)² + k
Vertex: (h, k)

Complex Numbers:
i = √(−1), i² = −1
(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i
Conjugate of a + bi = a − bi
lessons.content:
Vertex form y = a(x−h)² + k makes graphing quadratics easy — the vertex is right there at (h, k)! 'a' controls the width and direction (opens up if positive, down if negative).

When the discriminant is negative, solutions involve complex numbers. The imaginary unit i = √(−1), so i² = −1. Complex numbers have the form a + bi, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part.

Adding/subtracting complex numbers works like combining like terms. Multiplying uses FOIL (replace i² with −1). The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate always gives a real number!
steps: To graph: identify vertex (h, k) and direction from vertex form
For complex solutions: express using i where needed
Add complex numbers: (a+bi) + (c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i
Multiply using FOIL, then replace i² with −1
Simplify to standard form a + bi

examples.title: Vertex Form Graphing
examples.text: y = −2(x − 1)² + 4: Vertex at (1, 4). Opens downward (a = −2). Narrower than parent (|a| > 1).

lessons.tip: The complex conjugate trick: (a+bi)(a−bi) = a² + b² (always real!). This is how we divide complex numbers — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator to rationalize it.

quiz.q: The vertex of y = 2(x + 3)² − 1 is at:
quiz.explanation: Vertex form: a(x−h)²+k with h=−3, k=−1. Vertex: (−3, −1).

quiz.q: What is i²?
quiz.explanation: By definition, i = √(−1), so i² = −1.

quiz.q: Simplify: (2 + i)(2 − i)
quiz.explanation: FOIL: 4 − 2i + 2i − i² = 4 − (−1) = 5. This is the conjugate product!

quiz.q: If y = −(x − 2)² + 5, the parabola:
quiz.explanation: Negative a → opens down. Vertex at (2, 5).

lessons.title: Polynomial Functions & Division
lessons.description: Perform polynomial division and apply the Remainder and Factor Theorems!
lessons.formula:
Remainder Theorem:
f(c) = remainder when divided by (x − c)

Factor Theorem:
(x − c) is a factor of f(x) if f(c) = 0

End behavior:
Leading coeff positive, even degree → both up
Leading coeff negative, odd degree → left up, right down
lessons.content:
Polynomial long division divides polynomials just like regular long division. Synthetic division is a shortcut when dividing by (x − c) — it's faster and less error-prone.

The Remainder Theorem says f(c) equals the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x − c). The Factor Theorem says (x − c) is a factor if and only if f(c) = 0. These connect evaluation with factoring!

End behavior describes what happens to the graph as x → ∞ and x → −∞. It depends on the leading coefficient's sign and the degree's parity. A degree-n polynomial can have up to n−1 turning points.
steps: Set up long division or synthetic division
Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down (repeat)
The remainder is the last number (or f(c) by Remainder Theorem)
If f(c) = 0, then (x − c) is a factor by Factor Theorem
Determine end behavior from leading coefficient and degree

examples.title: Synthetic Division: x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6 ÷ (x − 2)
examples.text: Coefficients: 1, 2, −5, −6. Synthetic with 2: bring 1, multiply 2, add 4, multiply 8, add 3, multiply 6, add 0. Quotient: x² + 4x + 3, remainder 0.

examples.title: Factor Theorem: Is (x−3) a factor of x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6?
examples.text: Evaluate f(3) = 27 − 18 − 15 + 6 = 0. Since f(3) = 0, yes, (x−3) is a factor!

lessons.tip: Use the Rational Root Theorem to list POSSIBLE rational roots: factors of the constant term divided by factors of the leading coefficient. Test these with synthetic division — if the remainder is 0, you found a root AND a factor!

quiz.q: By the Remainder Theorem, f(2) equals the remainder when dividing by:
quiz.explanation: f(c) is the remainder when dividing by (x − c). So f(2) is the remainder when dividing by (x − 2).

quiz.q: If f(5) = 0, which is a factor of f(x)?
quiz.explanation: By the Factor Theorem, since f(5) = 0, (x − 5) is a factor.

quiz.q: A 4th-degree polynomial can have at most how many turning points?
quiz.explanation: A degree-n polynomial has at most n−1 turning points. For n=4: at most 3.

quiz.q: What is the end behavior of f(x) = 2x³?
quiz.explanation: Positive leading coefficient, odd degree: falls left, rises right.

lessons.title: Rational Expressions & Equations
lessons.description: Simplify, multiply, divide, and solve rational expressions and equations!
lessons.formula:
Simplifying:
Factor numerator and denominator,
cancel common factors

Solving: Multiply by LCD to clear
fractions, check for extraneous
solutions (zeros of denominators)
lessons.content:
Rational expressions are fractions with polynomials in the numerator and denominator. You simplify them the same way as regular fractions — factor and cancel common factors. But remember: you can only cancel FACTORS, not individual terms!

To add or subtract rational expressions with different denominators, find the Least Common Denominator (LCD). To solve rational equations, multiply both sides by the LCD to eliminate fractions.

Extraneous solutions can appear when solving — they make a denominator zero. ALWAYS check your answers by plugging them back into the original equation!
steps: Factor all numerators and denominators completely
Cancel any common factors between numerator and denominator
For addition/subtraction: find the LCD and rewrite with common denominator
For equations: multiply by LCD, solve the resulting polynomial equation
Check all solutions — discard any that make a denominator zero
lessons.tip: The #1 trap in rational expressions: canceling TERMS instead of FACTORS. (x+3)/(x²−9) does NOT simplify to 1/(x−3)... wait, actually x²−9 = (x+3)(x−3), so you CAN cancel (x+3). Always factor FIRST, then cancel!

quiz.q: Simplify: (x²−9)/(x+3)
What must you check for when solving rational equations?
quiz.explanation: Solutions that make denominators zero are extraneous and must be discarded.

quiz.q: The LCD of 1/(x+1) and 1/x is:
quiz.explanation: LCD is the product of the different denominators: x(x+1).

quiz.q: Simplify: 6x²/(3x)
quiz.explanation: 6x²/(3x) = (6/3)(x²/x) = 2x. Cancel common factors.

lessons.title: Exponential & Logarithmic Functions
lessons.description: Work with exponential growth/decay and logarithmic functions!
lessons.formula:
Exponential Growth: y = a(1 + r)ᵗ
Exponential Decay: y = a(1 − r)ᵗ

Logarithm: log_b(x) = y means bʸ = x
Properties:
log(xy) = log(x) + log(y)
log(x/y) = log(x) − log(y)
log(xⁿ) = n·log(x)
lessons.content:
Exponential functions have the variable in the exponent: y = a·bˣ. When b > 1, the function shows exponential growth (rapidly increasing). When 0 < b < 1, it shows exponential decay (rapidly decreasing). The graph always has a horizontal asymptote.

A logarithm is the inverse of an exponent: log_b(x) = y means bʸ = x. If 2³ = 8, then log₂(8) = 3. Common logarithms use base 10 (log), natural logarithms use base e (ln).

Logarithmic properties let you expand, condense, and solve equations. The change of base formula lets you evaluate any logarithm using a calculator: log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b).
steps: For exponential functions: identify the base (growth if >1, decay if <1)
The y-intercept is always at (0, a) since a·b⁰ = a
For logarithms: convert between log and exponential form
Use properties to expand or condense logarithmic expressions
To solve: rewrite log equation as exponential, or vice versa

examples.title: Exponential Growth
examples.text: A population of 500 grows at 10% per year. Formula: P = 500(1.1)ᵗ. After 5 years: P = 500(1.1)⁵ ≈ 805.

examples.title: Solving: log₂(32) = x
examples.text: Convert: 2ˣ = 32. Since 2⁵ = 32, x = 5. So log₂(32) = 5.

lessons.tip: The 'exponential' always wins in the long run! Both exponential growth and decay are MUCH more dramatic than linear change. A doubling time creates a surprisingly fast increase: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128... after just 7 doublings, you have 128x the original!

quiz.q: log₃(81) = ?
Solve: 2ˣ = 16
log(ab) = ?
quiz.explanation: The product rule: log(ab) = log(a) + log(b).

quiz.q: Is y = 0.5ˣ growth or decay?
quiz.explanation: Base 0.5 is between 0 and 1, so it's exponential decay.

lessons.title: Sequences & Series
lessons.description: Work with arithmetic and geometric sequences and their series!
lessons.formula:
Arithmetic nth term:
aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d

Arithmetic Sum:
Sₙ = n/2 · (a₁ + aₙ)

Geometric nth term:
aₙ = a₁ · rⁿ⁻¹

Geometric Sum:
Sₙ = a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)
lessons.content:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. An arithmetic sequence adds a constant difference d each time (2, 5, 8, 11... with d = 3). A geometric sequence multiplies by a constant ratio r each time (3, 6, 12, 24... with r = 2).

A series is the sum of a sequence's terms. The sum formula for arithmetic series averages the first and last terms, then multiplies by the number of terms. For geometric series, there's a convenient formula.

An infinite geometric series converges (has a finite sum) only when |r| < 1. The sum is S = a₁/(1−r). This concept is essential in calculus and many applications.
steps: Identify if the sequence is arithmetic (constant addition) or geometric (constant multiplication)
Find the common difference d or common ratio r
Use the nth term formula to find any term
Use the sum formula to find the sum of n terms
For infinite geometric: check if |r| < 1 for convergence
lessons.tip: Quick check: is a sequence arithmetic? Subtract consecutive terms — if the differences are the same, YES. Is it geometric? Divide consecutive terms — if the ratios are the same, YES. If neither, it's neither type!

quiz.q: Find the 10th term: 5, 9, 13, 17...
What is the common ratio of 1, 3, 9, 27...?
Does the infinite series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... converge?
quiz.explanation: r = 1/2, |r| < 1, so it converges. Sum = 1/(1−1/2) = 2.

quiz.q: Sum of first 20 terms of 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + ...

lessons.title: Radical Functions & Rational Exponents
lessons.description: Simplify radical expressions and understand rational exponents!
lessons.formula:
Rational Exponents:
x^(1/n) = ⁿ√x
x^(m/n) = (ⁿ√x)ᵐ

Properties:
ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b
ⁿ√(a/b) = ⁿ√a / ⁿ√b
lessons.content:
Rational exponents connect radicals and exponents. x^(1/2) = √x, x^(1/3) = ³√x. More generally, x^(m/n) means 'take the nth root, then raise to the mth power' — or vice versa (the order doesn't matter).

When simplifying radicals, factor out perfect squares (or cubes, etc.) from under the radical sign. For √72 = √(36·2) = 6√2. Always simplify to lowest radical form.

Solving radical equations requires squaring (or cubing) both sides to eliminate the radical. But this can introduce extraneous solutions, so ALWAYS check your answers in the original equation!
steps: Convert between radical and exponent notation as needed
Simplify radicals by factoring out perfect powers
When solving radical equations, isolate the radical first
Raise both sides to the appropriate power to eliminate the radical
CHECK all solutions — squaring can introduce extraneous ones

examples.title: Simplifying: √48
examples.text: √48 = √(16·3) = √16 · √3 = 4√3. Factor out the perfect square!

examples.title: Rational Exponents: 27^(2/3)
examples.text: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 3² = 9. Take the cube root, then square the result.

lessons.tip: A handy way to remember: x^(m/n) — the denominator (bottom) is the ROOT and the numerator (top) is the POWER. Think: 'down under, up top' — the root is under (in the radical) and the power is up (as an exponent).

quiz.q: Simplify: √50
What is 16^(3/4)?
Solve: √(x + 3) = 5
quiz.explanation: Square both sides: x + 3 = 25. x = 22. Check: √25 = 5 ✓

quiz.q: x^(1/5) is the same as:

lessons.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
lessons.description: Explore right triangle trigonometry with sine, cosine, and tangent!
lessons.formula:
SOH-CAH-TOA (for acute angles in right triangles):

sin(θ) = Opposite / Hypotenuse
cos(θ) = Adjacent / Hypotenuse
tan(θ) = Opposite / Adjacent

Inverse functions to find angles:
θ = arcsin(O/H) = sin⁻¹(O/H)
θ = arccos(A/H) = cos⁻¹(A/H)
θ = arctan(O/A) = tan⁻¹(O/A)

Common trig values:
sin(30°) = 1/2, cos(30°) = √3/2, tan(30°) = 1/√3
sin(45°) = √2/2, cos(45°) = √2/2, tan(45°) = 1
sin(60°) = √3/2, cos(60°) = 1/2, tan(60°) = √3
lessons.content:
Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that studies the relationships between angles and sides of triangles. In a right triangle, the three primary trigonometric ratios — sine, cosine, and tangent — relate an acute angle to the lengths of the triangle's sides. These ratios are constant for a given angle, regardless of the triangle's size. The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA helps you remember: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent.

To use these ratios, you must correctly identify which side is opposite the angle (the side across from the angle), which side is adjacent (the side next to the angle that is not the hypotenuse), and which side is the hypotenuse (always opposite the right angle, the longest side). For a given angle θ in a right triangle, the opposite and adjacent sides change depending on which acute angle you choose, but the hypotenuse is always the same. This distinction is critical and a common source of error.

Trigonometric ratios are used in two main ways. First, if you know an angle, you can find a ratio using a calculator (in degree mode). Second, if you know two sides of a right triangle, you can find an angle using the inverse trigonometric functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹). Applications include finding heights of buildings, calculating distances in navigation, analyzing forces in physics, and designing structures in engineering. The common angle values for 30°, 45°, and 60° connect directly to the special right triangles from the previous lesson.
steps: Label the right triangle: mark the right angle, identify the hypotenuse (always longest, opposite 90°)
Identify the angle of interest (θ) and label the opposite side and adjacent side relative to it
Decide which trig ratio to use based on the sides you know and the side you need to find
Set up the equation using SOH, CAH, or TOA
Solve for the unknown side or angle
If finding an angle, use the inverse function (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, or tan⁻¹) and ensure your calculator is in degree mode

examples.title: Example 1: Finding a Side Using Sine
examples.text:
In right ΔABC, ∠A = 35°, the hypotenuse BC = 12 cm. Find the length of the opposite side AB.

Step 1: We know the angle (35°) and the hypotenuse (12). We need the opposite side.
Step 2: Use sine: sin(35°) = opposite/hypotenuse = AB/12
Step 3: AB = 12 × sin(35°) = 12 × 0.5736 ≈ 6.88 cm
The side AB is approximately 6.88 cm.

examples.title: Example 2: Finding an Angle Using Inverse Tangent
examples.text:
A ramp rises 3 feet over a horizontal distance of 10 feet. What angle does the ramp make with the ground?

Step 1: The opposite side = 3 ft (rise), adjacent side = 10 ft (run).
Step 2: Use tangent: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = 3/10 = 0.3
Step 3: θ = tan⁻¹(0.3) ≈ 16.7°
The ramp makes an angle of approximately 16.7° with the ground.

lessons.tip: The most common mistake in trigonometry is confusing the opposite and adjacent sides. Remember: "opposite" means across from the angle you're working with, and "adjacent" means next to it (but never the hypotenuse). Before setting up any ratio, take two seconds to point at the angle, trace to the opposite side, and trace to the adjacent side.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, which ratio does SOH-CAH-TOA tell you for sine?
quiz.explanation: SOH stands for Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse. The opposite side is across from the angle of interest, and the hypotenuse is always the longest side.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, cos(θ) = 0.6 and the hypotenuse is 10. What is the length of the adjacent side?
quiz.explanation: cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse, so 0.6 = adjacent/10. Therefore, adjacent = 10 × 0.6 = 6.

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs of 3 and 4. What is tan(θ) where θ is the angle opposite the side of length 3?
quiz.explanation: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = 3/4. The opposite side is 3 and the adjacent side is 4 (relative to angle θ).

lessons.title: Linear Functions & Inequalities Review
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of linear functions & inequalities review
lessons.formula:
Slope-Intercept Form:  y = mx + b
Point-Slope Form:     y - y₁ = m(x - x₁)
Standard Form:        Ax + By = C
Slope formula:         m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁)
Inequality: if m > 0, graph above line; if m < 0, graph below
lessons.content:
A linear function has the form f(x) = mx + b, where m is the slope (rate of change) and b is the y-intercept. The graph is always a straight line. When we extend this to linear inequalities, we replace = with <, >, ≤, or ≥, and the solution is a half-plane (all points on one side of the boundary line).

To graph a linear inequality, first graph the boundary line as a solid line (for ≤ or ≥) or a dashed line (for < or >). Then shade the half-plane that satisfies the inequality. A reliable test is to substitute (0, 0) into the inequality; if it holds, shade the side containing the origin (provided the line doesn't pass through the origin).

Systems of linear inequalities involve shading the intersection of two or more half-planes. The feasible region is where all shaded regions overlap. These skills are essential for linear programming and optimization problems in pre-calculus and calculus.
steps: Rewrite the inequality in slope-intercept form (solve for y).
Graph the boundary line: solid if ≤/≥, dashed if </>.
Test a point (usually the origin) in the inequality.
Shade the half-plane that makes the inequality true.
For a system, repeat for each inequality and identify the overlap.

examples.title: Graphing 2x + 3y ≤ 12
examples.text: Solve for y: 3y ≤ -2x + 12 → y ≤ (-2/3)x + 4. Graph the solid line through (0, 4) and (6, 0). Test (0,0): 0 ≤ 12 is true, so shade below the line.

examples.title: System: y ≥ x + 1 and y < -x + 5
examples.text: Graph y = x + 1 (solid) and y = -x + 5 (dashed). The feasible region is the triangle where the shading overlaps, with vertices at (-2, 3), (2, 3), and (0, 1). The solution set is all points inside and on the first boundary.

lessons.tip: When graphing linear inequalities, always use the origin (0, 0) as your test point unless the boundary line passes through it. If the origin doesn't work, pick any convenient point like (1, 0) or (0, 1).

quiz.q: What does the graph of y > 2x - 3 look like?
options: A solid line with shading above it
A dashed line with shading below it
A dashed line with shading above it
A solid line with shading below it
quiz.explanation: Because the inequality is strict (>), the boundary line is dashed. Since y is greater than the expression, shade above the line.

quiz.q: Find the slope and y-intercept of 4x - 2y = 10.
quiz.explanation: Solving for y: -2y = -4x + 10 → y = 2x - 5. So m = 2 and b = -5.

quiz.q: Which test point would you use for the inequality x - y > 0?
quiz.explanation: The origin (0, 0) gives 0 - 0 = 0, which is not > 0. Use (0, 1) instead: 0 - 1 = -1 ≠ true, so try (1, 0): 1 - 0 = 1 > 0 is true.

quiz.q: The feasible region of a system of two linear inequalities is:
options: The union of the two half-planes
The intersection of the two half-planes
quiz.explanation: The solution to a system is the intersection — the region where both inequalities are simultaneously true.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Functions & Graphs
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of absolute value functions & graphs
lessons.formula:
Parent function:      f(x) = |x|
General form:         f(x) = a|x - h| + k
Vertex:               (h, k)
Domain:               (-∞, ∞)
Range (a > 0):        [k, ∞)
Range (a < 0):        (-∞, k]
lessons.content:
The absolute value function f(x) = |x| outputs the distance of x from zero, so it is always non-negative. Its graph is a V-shape with its lowest point at the vertex (0, 0). The function is defined piecewise: f(x) = x if x ≥ 0, and f(x) = -x if x < 0.

Transformations of the parent function follow the general form f(x) = a|x - h| + k. The coefficient |a| controls the steepness of the V: larger |a| means a narrower V, while 0 < |a| < 1 produces a wider V. If a < 0, the graph is reflected across the x-axis (opens downward). The values h and k shift the vertex to (h, k), giving horizontal and vertical translations respectively.

Understanding absolute value graphs is crucial for solving absolute value equations and inequalities. The vertex tells you the minimum (or maximum) value and the axis of symmetry divides the graph into two mirror-image halves.
steps: Identify the vertex (h, k) from the equation f(x) = a|x - h| + k.
Determine whether the graph opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0).
Find the axis of symmetry: the vertical line x = h.
Plot the vertex and two points on each side by substituting x-values.
Connect the points with two straight rays forming the V-shape.

examples.title: Graph f(x) = -2|x - 3| + 1
examples.text: Vertex: (3, 1). Opens downward since a = -2 < 0. Axis of symmetry: x = 3. Points: x=2 → f = -2|2-3|+1 = -2+1 = -1; x=4 → f = -2|4-3|+1 = -1. The V opens downward with vertex at (3, 1).

examples.title: Graph f(x) = |x + 2|
examples.text: Rewrite as f(x) = |x - (-2)|. Vertex: (-2, 0). Opens upward (a = 1). Axis of symmetry: x = -2. Points: x=-3 → f = 1; x=-1 → f = 1; x=-4 → f = 2.

lessons.tip: When solving absolute value equations like |x - 3| = 5, remember to split into two cases: x - 3 = 5 (giving x = 8) and x - 3 = -5 (giving x = -2). Always check both solutions!

quiz.q: What is the vertex of f(x) = 3|x + 1| - 4?
quiz.explanation: Rewrite as f(x) = 3|x - (-1)| + (-4), so h = -1 and k = -4. The vertex is (-1, -4).

quiz.q: Which transformation reflects the graph across the x-axis?
quiz.explanation: A negative coefficient (a < 0) reflects the graph. f(x) = -|x| opens downward.

quiz.q: What is the range of f(x) = -|x - 2| + 7?
quiz.explanation: Since a = -1 < 0, the V opens downward with vertex at (2, 7). The range is (-∞, 7].

quiz.q: Solve |2x - 6| = 10. What are the solutions?

quiz.title: Matrices and Operations
quiz.description: Add, subtract, and multiply matrices; understand matrix dimensions
quiz.formula:
Matrix Addition/Subtraction:
If A = [a_ij] and B = [b_ij] have the same dimensions m × n:
(A ± B)_ij = a_ij ± b_ij

Matrix Multiplication:
If A is m × n and B is n × p, then C = AB is m × p:
c_ij = Σ(k=1 to n) a_ik × b_kj
quiz.content:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. The dimensions are written as m × n, where m is the number of rows and n is the number of columns. Each individual number is called an element.

Addition and subtraction require the same dimensions—you add or subtract corresponding elements. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by a constant. Matrix multiplication requires the number of columns in the first matrix to equal the number of rows in the second. The element at row i, column j of the product is the dot product of row i of the first matrix with column j of the second.
steps: Determine the dimensions of each matrix (rows × columns)
For addition/subtraction: verify both matrices have the same dimensions
For multiplication: verify columns of A = rows of B; result is rows of A × columns of B
Add, subtract, or multiply element by element according to the operation
Write the resulting matrix with the correct dimensions

quiz.q: What are the dimensions of the result when multiplying a 3 × 2 matrix by a 2 × 4 matrix?

quiz.explanation: Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by the scalar. 3A means every element of A is multiplied by 3.

quiz.title: Determinants and Inverses
quiz.description: Find determinants of 2x2 and 3x3 matrices and find inverse matrices
quiz.formula:
Determinant of 2 × 2:
|A| = ad − bc where A = [[a, b], [c, d]]

Determinant of 3 × 3:
|A| = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg)

Inverse of 2 × 2:
A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) × [[d, −b], [−c, a]]

Condition: A⁻¹ exists only if |A| ≠ 0
quiz.content:
The determinant of a square matrix is a single number that reveals whether the matrix is invertible. For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc. For a 3 × 3 matrix, use cofactor expansion along any row or column. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular (not invertible).

The inverse matrix A⁻¹ is the matrix that, when multiplied by A, gives the identity matrix I. For a 2 × 2 matrix, the inverse is calculated using the adjugate formula. A matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Inverse matrices are essential for solving systems of equations using matrix methods.

Calculate the determinant using the appropriate formula
If |A| = 0, the matrix has no inverse (singular)
If |A| ≠ 0, find the inverse using the adjugate formula or row reduction
Verify: A × A⁻¹ should equal the identity matrix I

examples.title: Singular Matrix Check
examples.text: B = [[2, 4], [1, 2]]. |B| = 2×2 − 4×1 = 4 − 4 = 0. Since |B| = 0, B is singular and has no inverse.

quiz.tip: A quick way to check if a 2 × 2 matrix is invertible: if the rows (or columns) are proportional, the determinant is zero and there is no inverse. In the singular example, row 2 is exactly half of row 1!

quiz.q: Find the determinant of [[5, 3], [2, 4]].
If |A| = 0, what can you conclude?

quiz.q: What is the identity matrix for 2 × 2 matrices?
quiz.explanation: The identity matrix I has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else: [[1, 0], [0, 1]].

quiz.title: Conic Sections
quiz.description: Identify and graph circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas from equations
quiz.formula:
Circle: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
Ellipse: (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1
Parabola: (x − h)² = 4p(y − k)
Hyperbola: (x − h)²/a² − (y − k)²/b² = 1

Eccentricity: e = c/a
Circle: e=0, Ellipse: 0<e<1, Parabola: e=1, Hyperbola: e>1
quiz.content:
Conic sections are curves formed by intersecting a plane with a double cone. A circle results when the plane is perpendicular to the axis, an ellipse when angled, a parabola when parallel to the side, and a hyperbola when steeper. Each has a standard equation revealing key features.

To identify a conic from its general equation Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0, look at A and C. If A = C, it is a circle. If same sign but A ≠ C, it is an ellipse. If one is zero, it is a parabola. If opposite signs, it is a hyperbola. Completing the square converts general to standard form.
steps: Identify the conic type from the equation's coefficients
Complete the square to convert to standard form
Identify center (h,k), radii a and b, or focal parameter p
Plot the center and key points (vertices, co-vertices, foci)
Sketch the curve using symmetry and the key points

examples.title: Identifying and Graphing an Ellipse
examples.text: x²/25 + y²/9 = 1. Ellipse centered at origin with a²=25, b²=9, so a=5, b=3. Vertices at (±5, 0), co-vertices at (0, ±3). c = √(25−9) = 4, so foci at (±4, 0).

examples.title: Converting Parabola to Standard Form
examples.text: y = x² − 6x + 2. Complete the square: y = (x² − 6x + 9) − 9 + 2, so y = (x − 3)² − 7. Parabola with vertex at (3, −7), opening upward.

quiz.tip: Remember the discriminant: B² − 4AC. If < 0, ellipse or circle. If = 0, parabola. If > 0, hyperbola. This works even for rotated conics when B ≠ 0!

quiz.q: What conic section is described by x² + y² = 16?
quiz.explanation: Both x² and y² have the same coefficient (1), so this is a circle with center (0,0) and radius 4.

quiz.q: What is the center of (x − 2)²/9 + (y + 1)²/16 = 1?
quiz.explanation: Standard form (x−h)²/a² + (y−k)²/b² = 1 gives center (h,k) = (2, −1). Note the sign flip on k.

quiz.q: Which conic has A and C with opposite signs?
quiz.explanation: In a hyperbola, the squared terms have opposite signs, so A and C have opposite signs.

quiz.title: Binomial Theorem
quiz.description: Expand binomials using Pascal's Triangle and the binomial theorem formula
quiz.formula:
Binomial Theorem:
(a + b)^n = Σ(k=0 to n) C(n,k) × a^(n−k) × b^k

Binomial Coefficient:
C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!)

Pascal's Triangle rows:
0: 1
1: 1  1
2: 1  2  1
3: 1  3  3  1
4: 1  4  6  4  1
quiz.content:
The Binomial Theorem provides a formula for expanding (a + b)n without multiplying repeatedly. Each term has the form C(n,k) × an−k × bk, where C(n,k) is the binomial coefficient from row n of Pascal's Triangle.

Pascal's Triangle is a triangular arrangement where each entry is the sum of the two above it. Row 4 gives coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, so (a + b)4 = a4 + 4a3b + 6a2b2 + 4ab3 + b4. The theorem works for any positive integer n.
steps: Identify n (the power) from (a + b)^n
Find the binomial coefficients using Pascal's Triangle or C(n,k)
Write each term: C(n,k) × a^(n−k) × b^k for k = 0 to n
Combine like terms if necessary
Simplify the final expression

examples.title: Expanding (x + 2)³
examples.text: Row 3 of Pascal's Triangle: 1, 3, 3, 1. (x + 2)³ = 1·x³·2⁰ + 3·x²·2¹ + 3·x¹·2² + 1·x⁰·2³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

examples.title: Finding a Specific Term
examples.text: Find the 3rd term of (2x − 3)⁵. The 3rd term uses k=2: C(5,2)(2x)³(−3)² = 10 × 8x³ × 9 = 720x³.

quiz.tip: To find a specific term, remember the term number is k+1 (since k starts at 0). The kth term always has b raised to the power k. Watch out for negative signs in b — they alternate the terms!

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (x + 1)⁴?
quiz.explanation: Row 4 of Pascal's Triangle: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. The coefficient of x² (where k=2) is C(4,2) = 6.

quiz.q: How many terms are in the expansion of (a + b)⁷?
quiz.explanation: The expansion of (a + b)^n has n + 1 terms. For n = 7, there are 8 terms.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the coefficients in row 3 of Pascal's Triangle?
quiz.explanation: Row 3 is 1, 3, 3, 1. Sum = 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8. In general, the sum of row n is 2^n.

quiz.title: Probability Distributions
quiz.description: Calculate mean and standard deviation of probability distributions
quiz.formula:
Expected Value (Mean):
μ = Σ x_i × P(x_i)

Variance:
σ² = Σ (x_i − μ)² × P(x_i)

Standard Deviation:
σ = √(σ²)

Conditions:
Σ P(x_i) = 1  and  0 ≤ P(x_i) ≤ 1
quiz.content:
A probability distribution lists all possible outcomes of a random variable with their probabilities. A discrete random variable takes countable values. Every probability must be between 0 and 1, and they must sum to exactly 1.

The expected value μ is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and sum. The variance σ² measures spread from the mean. The standard deviation σ = √(σ²) has the same units as the data, making it more interpretable.

Verify that all probabilities sum to 1
Calculate the expected value: μ = Σ x × P(x)
Calculate the variance: σ² = Σ (x − μ)² × P(x)
Take the square root to get standard deviation: σ = √(σ²)

examples.title: Expected Value of a Game
examples.text: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2, $5 with probability 0.3, and $0 with probability 0.5. μ = 10(0.2) + 5(0.3) + 0(0.5) = 2 + 1.5 + 0 = $3.50.

quiz.tip: The expected value is NOT necessarily a possible outcome! If you roll a die, the expected value is 3.5, but you can never roll a 3.5. Think of it as the average over many, many trials.

quiz.q: A coin flip pays $5 for heads and −$2 for tails. What is the expected value?
What must the probabilities in a distribution sum to?
quiz.explanation: The sum of all probabilities in a valid probability distribution must equal exactly 1.

quiz.q: If variance is 25, what is the standard deviation?

quiz.title: Permutations
quiz.description: Calculate permutations using nPr and factorial notation
quiz.formula:
Permutation Formula:
P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!

Factorial:
n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 2 × 1

Examples:
0! = 1, 1! = 1, 5! = 120

P(5, 3) = 5! / 2! = 60
P(n, n) = n!
quiz.content:
A permutation is an arrangement of objects where order matters. When selecting r objects from n distinct objects and arranging them in order, the number of permutations is P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!. For example, arranging 3 books from a collection of 5 gives P(5,3) = 60 different arrangements.

The factorial function n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n. Factorials grow extremely quickly: 10! = 3,628,800. A special case is 0! = 1. Permutations are used when every position is unique—like first, second, third place in a race, or creating PIN codes.

Determine r (number of positions to fill)
Apply the formula: P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!
Calculate the factorials in numerator and denominator
Simplify and compute the final answer

examples.text: 8 runners compete for gold, silver, bronze. P(8,3) = 8!/(8−3)! = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 possible podium arrangements.

examples.title: Arranging All Letters

quiz.tip: Permutation means ORDER matters. If the question asks about presidents, rankings, passwords, or seating arrangements where position is important, use permutations. ABC and BAC are DIFFERENT permutations but the SAME combination.

quiz.q: P(6, 2) equals what?
How many 4-digit PIN codes can be made using digits 0–9 if no digit repeats?
What is the value of 0!?
quiz.explanation: By definition and mathematical convention, 0! = 1. This is necessary for permutation formulas to work correctly.

quiz.description: Calculate combinations using nCr formula and understand when order matters vs doesn't
quiz.formula:

C(n, r) = n! / (r!(n − r)!)

Relationship to Permutations:
C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!

Examples:
C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! × 3!) = 10
C(10, 3) = 10! / (3! × 7!) = 120

Symmetry: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r)
quiz.content:
A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter. When choosing r objects from n distinct objects, the number of combinations is C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!). For example, choosing 2 friends from 5 gives C(5,2) = 10 different groups.

The key distinction: picking a president and vice-president is a permutation (ABC ≠ BAC). Picking 2 team captains is a combination (ABC = BAC). Combinations are always ≤ permutations for the same n and r, because C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r! accounts for all r! ways to rearrange the selection.

Decide: does order matter? If yes use P(n,r); if no use C(n,r)
Apply C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) or use Pascal's Triangle
Simplify by canceling common factors before multiplying
Check: C(n,r) should always equal C(n, n−r)

examples.title: Choosing a Committee
examples.text: From 7 people, choose 3 for a committee. C(7,3) = 7!/(3! × 4!) = (7×6×5)/(3×2×1) = 35. Order does not matter for committee members.

examples.title: Permutation vs Combination
examples.text: 5 people: choosing 2 for president and VP = P(5,2) = 20. Choosing 2 for a team = C(5,2) = 10. The permutation is 2! = 2 times larger.

quiz.tip: Ask yourself: 'If I swap two items, is it a different answer?' If yes — permutation. If no — combination. A pizza with pepperoni and mushroom is the same as one with mushroom and pepperoni!

quiz.q: C(8, 3) equals what?
Choosing 5 cards from a 52-card deck is a permutation or combination?
quiz.explanation: A poker hand has no inherent order, so it is a combination: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960 possible hands.

quiz.q: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r) is which property?
quiz.explanation: The symmetry property: choosing r items is the same as leaving behind n−r items. C(7,2) = C(7,5) = 21.

quiz.title: Vectors
quiz.description: Represent vectors as ordered pairs, find magnitude, add and subtract vectors
quiz.formula:
Component Form: v = ⟨x, y⟩

Magnitude:
|v| = √(x² + y²)

Vector Addition:
⟨a, b⟩ + ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a+c, b+d⟩

Scalar Multiplication:
k × ⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨kx, ky⟩

Unit Vector:
û = v/|v|
quiz.content:
A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction. Vectors are represented as ordered pairs ⟨x, y⟩, where x is the horizontal component and y is the vertical component. The magnitude is |v| = √(x² + y²).

Vector addition combines vectors by adding corresponding components. Geometrically, this follows the tip-to-tail method. Scalar multiplication stretches or shrinks a vector. A unit vector has magnitude 1 and points in the same direction as the original.
steps: Write the vector in component form ⟨x, y⟩
Find magnitude: |v| = √(x² + y²)
To add vectors: add corresponding x and y components
To subtract vectors: subtract corresponding x and y components
To find the unit vector: divide each component by the magnitude

examples.title: Finding Magnitude
examples.text: v = ⟨3, 4⟩. |v| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The vector has length 5 units.

examples.title: Vector Addition
examples.text: a = ⟨2, −1⟩, b = ⟨4, 3⟩. a + b = ⟨2+4, −1+3⟩ = ⟨6, 2⟩. The resultant goes 6 right and 2 up.

quiz.tip: Think of vectors as displacement: 'walk 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north.' The magnitude is the straight-line distance home (5 blocks), and the direction is the angle. Components are the east/west and north/south steps!

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of ⟨5, 12⟩?

quiz.explanation: Add components: 3 + (−1) = 2, 2 + 5 = 7. Result: ⟨2, 7⟩.

quiz.q: What is the unit vector of ⟨0, 1⟩?
quiz.explanation: |⟨0, 1⟩| = 1, so the unit vector is already ⟨0, 1⟩. It has magnitude 1!

quiz.description: Convert between rectangular and polar coordinates and plot polar equations
quiz.formula:
Rectangular to Polar:
r = √(x² + y²)
θ = arctan(y/x)

Polar to Rectangular:
x = r cos(θ)
y = r sin(θ)

Note: Check quadrant when finding θ
Negative r: reflect through the origin
quiz.content:
Polar coordinates (r, θ) describe a point by its distance r from the origin (the pole) and the angle θ> measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis (polar axis). Unlike rectangular (x,y), polar uses distance and direction—like a radar screen.

To convert: x = r cos(θ) and y = r sin(θ) for polar to rectangular; r = √(x²+y²) with θ = arctan(y/x) for rectangular to polar. Be careful: arctan alone does not distinguish all quadrants. A negative r means go in the opposite direction: (−3, π/4) is the same as (3, 5π/4).

Find θ = arctan(y/x) and adjust for the correct quadrant
To convert (r,θ) to rectangular: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ)
When plotting: rotate by θ from the polar axis, then move r units along that direction
Remember: (r,θ) and (−r, θ + π) represent the same point

examples.title: Rectangular to Polar
examples.text: Point (−3, 3). r = √(9+9) = 3√2. θ = arctan(3/(−3)) in Quadrant II: θ = 3π/4. Polar form: (3√2, 3π/4).

quiz.tip: Always sketch the point first! If a point is in Quadrant II (negative x, positive y), arctan gives a Quadrant IV angle—you must add π to correct it. Visualizing prevents quadrant errors.

Convert (6, π) from polar to rectangular coordinates.
quiz.explanation: x = 6 cos(π) = 6(−1) = −6. y = 6 sin(π) = 0. Rectangular: (−6, 0).

quiz.explanation: (r,θ) = (−r, θ+π): (−2, π/3+π) = (−2, 4π/3) represents the same point.

quiz.title: Parametric Equations
quiz.description: Write and graph parametric equations, convert between parametric and rectangular
quiz.formula:
Parametric to Rectangular:
Given x = f(t), y = g(t),
solve for t in one equation
and substitute into the other.

Common Elimination:
x = r cos(t), y = r sin(t) → x² + y² = r² (circle)

x = v₀ cos(θ) × t

To eliminate the parameter, solve one equation for t and substitute into the other. For example, if x = 2t and y = t²+1, then t = x/2 and y = (x/2)²+1 = x²/4+1. The orientation (direction of increasing t) matters—the same curve traced in opposite directions has different parametric equations.

To eliminate: solve one equation for t, substitute into the other

quiz.q: If x = t + 1 and y = t², what is the rectangular equation?
quiz.explanation: From x = t + 1, t = x − 1. Substitute: y = (x − 1)².

quiz.q: x = 4 cos(t), y = 4 sin(t) describes what shape?
quiz.explanation: x²/16 + y²/16 = 1, so x² + y² = 16, a circle of radius 4.

quiz.q: What does the parameter t represent in projectile motion?
quiz.explanation: In physics, t typically represents time, and x and y represent position at that time.

The element at row i, column j of the product is the dot product of row i of the first matrix with column j of the second.

examples.text: y = x² − 6x + 2. Complete the square: y = (x² − 6x + 9) − 9 + 2, so y = (x − 3)² − 7. Parabola with vertex at (3, −7), opening upward.

quiz.tip: Remember the discriminant: B² − 4AC. If < 0, ellipse or circle. If = 0, parabola. If > 0, hyperbola. This works even for rotated conics when B ≠ 0!

quiz.q: What conic section is described by x² + y² = 16?
quiz.explanation: Both x² and y² have the same coefficient (1), so this is a circle with center (0,0) and radius 4.

quiz.q: What is the center of (x − 2)²/9 + (y + 1)²/16 = 1?
quiz.explanation: Standard form (x−h)²/a² + (y−k)²/b² = 1 gives center (h,k) = (2, −1). Note the sign flip on k.

quiz.q: Which conic has A and C with opposite signs?
quiz.explanation: In a hyperbola, the squared terms have opposite signs, so A and C have opposite signs.

quiz.title: Binomial Theorem
quiz.description: Expand binomials using Pascal's Triangle and the binomial theorem formula
quiz.formula:
Binomial Theorem:
(a + b)^n = Σ(k=0 to n) C(n,k) × a^(n−k) × b^k

Binomial Coefficient:
C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!)

Pascal's Triangle rows:
0: 1
1: 1  1
2: 1  2  1
3: 1  3  3  1
4: 1  4  6  4  1
quiz.content:
The Binomial Theorem provides a formula for expanding (a + b)n without multiplying repeatedly. Each term has the form C(n,k) × an−k × bk, where C(n,k) is the binomial coefficient from row n of Pascal's Triangle.

Pascal's Triangle is a triangular arrangement where each entry is the sum of the two above it. Row 4 gives coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, so (a + b)4 = a4 + 4a3b + 6a2b2 + 4ab3 + b4. The theorem works for any positive integer n.
steps: Identify n (the power) from (a + b)^n
Find the binomial coefficients using Pascal's Triangle or C(n,k)
Write each term: C(n,k) × a^(n−k) × b^k for k = 0 to n
Combine like terms if necessary
Simplify the final expression

examples.title: Expanding (x + 2)³
examples.text: Row 3 of Pascal's Triangle: 1, 3, 3, 1. (x + 2)³ = 1·x³·2⁰ + 3·x²·2¹ + 3·x¹·2² + 1·x⁰·2³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

examples.title: Finding a Specific Term
examples.text: Find the 3rd term of (2x − 3)⁵. The 3rd term uses k=2: C(5,2)(2x)³(−3)² = 10 × 8x³ × 9 = 720x³.

quiz.tip: To find a specific term, remember the term number is k+1 (since k starts at 0). The kth term always has b raised to the power k. Watch out for negative signs in b — they alternate the terms!

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (x + 1)⁴?
quiz.explanation: Row 4 of Pascal's Triangle: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. The coefficient of x² (where k=2) is C(4,2) = 6.

quiz.q: How many terms are in the expansion of (a + b)⁷?
quiz.explanation: The expansion of (a + b)^n has n + 1 terms. For n = 7, there are 8 terms.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the coefficients in row 3 of Pascal's Triangle?
quiz.explanation: Row 3 is 1, 3, 3, 1. Sum = 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8. In general, the sum of row n is 2^n.

quiz.title: Probability Distributions
quiz.description: Calculate mean and standard deviation of probability distributions
quiz.formula:
Expected Value (Mean):
μ = Σ x_i × P(x_i)

Variance:
σ² = Σ (x_i − μ)² × P(x_i)

Standard Deviation:
σ = √(σ²)

Conditions:
Σ P(x_i) = 1  and  0 ≤ P(x_i) ≤ 1
quiz.content:
A probability distribution lists all possible outcomes of a random variable with their probabilities. A discrete random variable takes countable values. Every probability must be between 0 and 1, and they must sum to exactly 1.

The expected value μ is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and sum. The variance σ² measures spread from the mean. The standard deviation σ = √(σ²) has the same units as the data, making it more interpretable.
steps: List all possible values and their probabilities
Verify that all probabilities sum to 1
Calculate the expected value: μ = Σ x × P(x)
Calculate the variance: σ² = Σ (x − μ)² × P(x)
Take the square root to get standard deviation: σ = √(σ²)

examples.title: Expected Value of a Game
examples.text: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2, $5 with probability 0.3, and $0 with probability 0.5. μ = 10(0.2) + 5(0.3) + 0(0.5) = 2 + 1.5 + 0 = $3.50.

quiz.tip: The expected value is NOT necessarily a possible outcome! If you roll a die, the expected value is 3.5, but you can never roll a 3.5. Think of it as the average over many, many trials.

quiz.q: A coin flip pays $5 for heads and −$2 for tails. What is the expected value?
What must the probabilities in a distribution sum to?
quiz.explanation: The sum of all probabilities in a valid probability distribution must equal exactly 1.

quiz.q: If variance is 25, what is the standard deviation?

quiz.title: Permutations
quiz.description: Calculate permutations using nPr and factorial notation
quiz.formula:
Permutation Formula:
P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!

Factorial:
n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 2 × 1

Examples:
0! = 1, 1! = 1, 5! = 120

P(5, 3) = 5! / 2! = 60
P(n, n) = n!
quiz.content:
A permutation is an arrangement of objects where order matters. When selecting r objects from n distinct objects and arranging them in order, the number of permutations is P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!. For example, arranging 3 books from a collection of 5 gives P(5,3) = 60 different arrangements.

The factorial function n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n. Factorials grow extremely quickly: 10! = 3,628,800. A special case is 0! = 1. Permutations are used when every position is unique—like first, second, third place in a race, or creating PIN codes.
steps: Determine n (total number of objects available)
Determine r (number of positions to fill)
Apply the formula: P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!
Calculate the factorials in numerator and denominator
Simplify and compute the final answer

examples.title: Arranging Runners on a Podium
examples.text: 8 runners compete for gold, silver, bronze. P(8,3) = 8!/(8−3)! = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 possible podium arrangements.

examples.title: Arranging All Letters
examples.text: How many ways to arrange 5 books on a shelf? P(5,5) = 5! = 120. When arranging all items, it is simply n!.

quiz.tip: Permutation means ORDER matters. If the question asks about presidents, rankings, passwords, or seating arrangements where position is important, use permutations. ABC and BAC are DIFFERENT permutations but the SAME combination.

quiz.q: P(6, 2) equals what?
How many 4-digit PIN codes can be made using digits 0–9 if no digit repeats?
What is the value of 0!?
quiz.explanation: By definition and mathematical convention, 0! = 1. This is necessary for permutation formulas to work correctly.

quiz.title: Combinations
quiz.description: Calculate combinations using nCr formula and understand when order matters vs doesn't
quiz.formula:
Combination Formula:
C(n, r) = n! / (r!(n − r)!)

Relationship to Permutations:
C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!

Examples:
C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! × 3!) = 10
C(10, 3) = 10! / (3! × 7!) = 120

Symmetry: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r)
quiz.content:
A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter. When choosing r objects from n distinct objects, the number of combinations is C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!). For example, choosing 2 friends from 5 gives C(5,2) = 10 different groups.

The key distinction: picking a president and vice-president is a permutation (ABC ≠ BAC). Picking 2 team captains is a combination (ABC = BAC). Combinations are always ≤ permutations for the same n and r, because C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r! accounts for all r! ways to rearrange the selection.
steps: Determine n (total objects) and r (objects being selected)
Decide: does order matter? If yes use P(n,r); if no use C(n,r)
Apply C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) or use Pascal's Triangle
Simplify by canceling common factors before multiplying
Check: C(n,r) should always equal C(n, n−r)

examples.title: Choosing a Committee
examples.text: From 7 people, choose 3 for a committee. C(7,3) = 7!/(3! × 4!) = (7×6×5)/(3×2×1) = 35. Order does not matter for committee members.

examples.title: Permutation vs Combination
examples.text: 5 people: choosing 2 for president and VP = P(5,2) = 20. Choosing 2 for a team = C(5,2) = 10. The permutation is 2! = 2 times larger.

quiz.tip: Ask yourself: 'If I swap two items, is it a different answer?' If yes — permutation. If no — combination. A pizza with pepperoni and mushroom is the same as one with mushroom and pepperoni!

quiz.q: C(8, 3) equals what?
Choosing 5 cards from a 52-card deck is a permutation or combination?
quiz.explanation: A poker hand has no inherent order, so it is a combination: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960 possible hands.

quiz.q: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r) is which property?
quiz.explanation: The symmetry property: choosing r items is the same as leaving behind n−r items. C(7,2) = C(7,5) = 21.

quiz.title: Vectors
quiz.description: Represent vectors as ordered pairs, find magnitude, add and subtract vectors
quiz.formula:
Component Form: v = ⟨x, y⟩

Magnitude:
|v| = √(x² + y²)

Vector Addition:
⟨a, b⟩ + ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a+c, b+d⟩

Scalar Multiplication:
k × ⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨kx, ky⟩

Unit Vector:
û = v/|v|
quiz.content:
A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction. Vectors are represented as ordered pairs ⟨x, y⟩, where x is the horizontal component and y is the vertical component. The magnitude is |v| = √(x² + y²).

Vector addition combines vectors by adding corresponding components. Geometrically, this follows the tip-to-tail method. Scalar multiplication stretches or shrinks a vector. A unit vector has magnitude 1 and points in the same direction as the original.
steps: Write the vector in component form ⟨x, y⟩
Find magnitude: |v| = √(x² + y²)
To add vectors: add corresponding x and y components
To subtract vectors: subtract corresponding x and y components
To find the unit vector: divide each component by the magnitude

examples.title: Finding Magnitude
examples.text: v = ⟨3, 4⟩. |v| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The vector has length 5 units.

examples.title: Vector Addition
examples.text: a = ⟨2, −1⟩, b = ⟨4, 3⟩. a + b = ⟨2+4, −1+3⟩ = ⟨6, 2⟩. The resultant goes 6 right and 2 up.

quiz.tip: Think of vectors as displacement: 'walk 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north.' The magnitude is the straight-line distance home (5 blocks), and the direction is the angle. Components are the east/west and north/south steps!

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of ⟨5, 12⟩?

quiz.explanation: Add components: 3 + (−1) = 2, 2 + 5 = 7. Result: ⟨2, 7⟩.

quiz.q: What is the unit vector of ⟨0, 1⟩?
quiz.explanation: |⟨0, 1⟩| = 1, so the unit vector is already ⟨0, 1⟩. It has magnitude 1!

quiz.title: Polar Coordinates
quiz.description: Convert between rectangular and polar coordinates and plot polar equations
quiz.formula:
Rectangular to Polar:
r = √(x² + y²)
θ = arctan(y/x)

Polar to Rectangular:
x = r cos(θ)
y = r sin(θ)

Note: Check quadrant when finding θ
Negative r: reflect through the origin
quiz.content:
Polar coordinates (r, θ) describe a point by its distance r from the origin (the pole) and the angle θ> measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis (polar axis). Unlike rectangular (x,y), polar uses distance and direction—like a radar screen.

To convert: x = r cos(θ) and y = r sin(θ) for polar to rectangular; r = √(x²+y²) with θ = arctan(y/x) for rectangular to polar. Be careful: arctan alone does not distinguish all quadrants. A negative r means go in the opposite direction: (−3, π/4) is the same as (3, 5π/4).
steps: To convert (x,y) to polar: find r = √(x² + y²)
Find θ = arctan(y/x) and adjust for the correct quadrant
To convert (r,θ) to rectangular: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ)
When plotting: rotate by θ from the polar axis, then move r units along that direction
Remember: (r,θ) and (−r, θ + π) represent the same point

examples.title: Rectangular to Polar
examples.text: Point (−3, 3). r = √(9+9) = 3√2. θ = arctan(3/(−3)) in Quadrant II: θ = 3π/4. Polar form: (3√2, 3π/4).

quiz.tip: Always sketch the point first! If a point is in Quadrant II (negative x, positive y), arctan gives a Quadrant IV angle—you must add π to correct it. Visualizing prevents quadrant errors.

quiz.q: Convert (2, 2) from rectangular to polar coordinates.
Convert (6, π) from polar to rectangular coordinates.
quiz.explanation: x = 6 cos(π) = 6(−1) = −6. y = 6 sin(π) = 0. Rectangular: (−6, 0).

quiz.q: Which point is the same as (2, π/3)?
quiz.explanation: (r,θ) = (−r, θ+π): (−2, π/3+π) = (−2, 4π/3) represents the same point.

quiz.title: Parametric Equations
quiz.description: Write and graph parametric equations, convert between parametric and rectangular
quiz.formula:
Parametric to Rectangular:
Given x = f(t), y = g(t),
solve for t in one equation
and substitute into the other.

Common Elimination:
x = r cos(t), y = r sin(t) → x² + y² = r² (circle)

Projectile:
x = v₀ cos(θ) × t
y = −½gt² + v₀ sin(θ) × t + h
quiz.content:
Parametric equations express x and y as functions of a parameter t. Instead of y = f(x), we write x = f(t) and y = g(t). This allows curves that fail the vertical line test and modeling motion over time.

To eliminate the parameter, solve one equation for t and substitute into the other. For example, if x = 2t and y = t²+1, then t = x/2 and y = (x/2)²+1 = x²/4+1. The orientation (direction of increasing t) matters—the same curve traced in opposite directions has different parametric equations.
steps: Identify the parametric equations x = f(t) and y = g(t)
Create a table of values by choosing t-values and computing x and y
Plot the (x, y) points to see the curve's shape
To eliminate: solve one equation for t, substitute into the other
Indicate orientation with arrows showing direction of increasing t

examples.title: Eliminating the Parameter
examples.text: x = 3 cos(t), y = 2 sin(t). Then (x/3)² + (y/2)² = cos²(t) + sin²(t) = 1. This is an ellipse: x²/9 + y²/4 = 1.

examples.title: Projectile Motion
examples.text: x = 50t, y = −16t² + 80t. Eliminate: t = x/50, y = −16(x/50)² + 80(x/50) = −16x²/2500 + 8x/5. A parabolic trajectory.

quiz.tip: When graphing parametric equations, always indicate direction with arrows. Two parametric equations might produce the same rectangular equation but trace the curve in different directions or at different speeds!

quiz.q: If x = t + 1 and y = t², what is the rectangular equation?
quiz.explanation: From x = t + 1, t = x − 1. Substitute: y = (x − 1)².

quiz.q: x = 4 cos(t), y = 4 sin(t) describes what shape?
quiz.explanation: x²/16 + y²/16 = 1, so x² + y² = 16, a circle of radius 4.

quiz.q: What does the parameter t represent in projectile motion?
quiz.explanation: In physics, t typically represents time, and x and y represent position at that time.

quiz.title: Matrices and Operations
quiz.description: Add, subtract, and multiply matrices; understand matrix dimensions
quiz.formula:
Matrix Addition/Subtraction:
If A = [a_ij] and B = [b_ij] have the same dimensions m × n:
(A ± B)_ij = a_ij ± b_ij

Matrix Multiplication:
If A is m × n and B is n × p, then C = AB is m × p:
c_ij = Σ(k=1 to n) a_ik × b_kj
quiz.content:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. The dimensions are written as m × n, where m is the number of rows and n is the number of columns. Each individual number is called an element.

Addition and subtraction require the same dimensions—you add or subtract corresponding elements. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by a constant. Matrix multiplication requires the number of columns in the first matrix to equal the number of rows in the second. The element at row i, column j of the product is the dot product of row i of the first matrix with column j of the second.
steps: Determine the dimensions of each matrix (rows × columns)
For addition/subtraction: verify both matrices have the same dimensions
For multiplication: verify columns of A = rows of B; result is rows of A × columns of B
Add, subtract, or multiply element by element according to the operation
Write the resulting matrix with the correct dimensions
quiz.tip: A quick check for matrix multiplication: if A is m × n and B is n × p, the result is always m × p. The 'middle' dimension n must match! Think of it as the inner dimensions canceling out.

quiz.q: What are the dimensions of the result when multiplying a 3 × 2 matrix by a 2 × 4 matrix?
quiz.explanation: The result has dimensions equal to the outer dimensions: rows of A (3) × columns of B (4) = 3 × 4.

quiz.q: Can you add a 2 × 3 matrix and a 3 × 2 matrix?
quiz.explanation: Matrices must have the exact same dimensions to be added. 2 × 3 ≠ 3 × 2, so they cannot be added directly.

quiz.q: If A is a 2 × 3 matrix, what is 3A?
options: Every element of A multiplied by 3
quiz.explanation: Scalar multiplication multiplies every element by the scalar. 3A means every element of A is multiplied by 3.

quiz.title: Determinants and Inverses
quiz.description: Find determinants of 2x2 and 3x3 matrices and find inverse matrices
quiz.formula:
Determinant of 2 × 2:
|A| = ad − bc where A = [[a, b], [c, d]]

Determinant of 3 × 3:
|A| = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg)

Inverse of 2 × 2:
A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) × [[d, −b], [−c, a]]

Condition: A⁻¹ exists only if |A| ≠ 0
quiz.content:
The determinant of a square matrix is a single number that reveals whether the matrix is invertible. For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc. For a 3 × 3 matrix, use cofactor expansion along any row or column. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular (not invertible).

The inverse matrix A⁻¹ is the matrix that, when multiplied by A, gives the identity matrix I. For a 2 × 2 matrix, the inverse is calculated using the adjugate formula. A matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Inverse matrices are essential for solving systems of equations using matrix methods.
steps: Check that the matrix is square (same number of rows and columns)
Calculate the determinant using the appropriate formula
If |A| = 0, the matrix has no inverse (singular)
If |A| ≠ 0, find the inverse using the adjugate formula or row reduction
Verify: A × A⁻¹ should equal the identity matrix I

examples.title: Singular Matrix Check
examples.text: B = [[2, 4], [1, 2]]. |B| = 2×2 − 4×1 = 4 − 4 = 0. Since |B| = 0, B is singular and has no inverse.

quiz.tip: A quick way to check if a 2 × 2 matrix is invertible: if the rows (or columns) are proportional, the determinant is zero and there is no inverse. In the singular example, row 2 is exactly half of row 1!

quiz.q: Find the determinant of [[5, 3], [2, 4]].
If |A| = 0, what can you conclude?
quiz.explanation: A determinant of zero means the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

quiz.q: What is the identity matrix for 2 × 2 matrices?
quiz.explanation: The identity matrix I has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else: [[1, 0], [0, 1]].

quiz.title: Conic Sections
quiz.description: Identify and graph circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas from equations
quiz.formula:
Circle: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
Ellipse: (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1
Parabola: (x − h)² = 4p(y − k)
Hyperbola: (x − h)²/a² − (y − k)²/b² = 1

Eccentricity: e = c/a
Circle: e=0, Ellipse: 0<e<1, Parabola: e=1, Hyperbola: e>1
quiz.content:
Conic sections are curves formed by intersecting a plane with a double cone. A circle results when the plane is perpendicular to the axis, an ellipse when angled, a parabola when parallel to the side, and a hyperbola when steeper. Each has a standard equation revealing key features.

To identify a conic from its general equation Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0, look at A and C. If A = C, it is a circle. If same sign but A ≠ C, it is an ellipse. If one is zero, it is a parabola. If opposite signs, it is a hyperbola. Completing the square converts general to standard form.
steps: Identify the conic type from the equation's coefficients
Complete the square to convert to standard form
Identify center (h,k), radii a and b, or focal parameter p
Plot the center and key points (vertices, co-vertices, foci)
Sketch the curve using symmetry and the key points
