The expected value μ is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and sum. The variance σ² measures spread from the mean. The standard deviation σ = √(σ²) has the same units as the data, making it more interpretable.
steps: List all possible values and their probabilities
Verify that all probabilities sum to 1
Calculate the expected value: μ = Σ x × P(x)
Calculate the variance: σ² = Σ (x − μ)² × P(x)
Take the square root to get standard deviation: σ = √(σ²)

examples.title: Expected Value of a Game
examples.text: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2, $5 with probability 0.3, and $0 with probability 0.5. μ = 10(0.2) + 5(0.3) + 0(0.5) = 2 + 1.5 + 0 = $3.50.

quiz.tip: The expected value is NOT necessarily a possible outcome! If you roll a die, the expected value is 3.5, but you can never roll a 3.5. Think of it as the average over many, many trials.

quiz.q: A coin flip pays $5 for heads and −$2 for tails. What is the expected value?
What must the probabilities in a distribution sum to?
quiz.explanation: The sum of all probabilities in a valid probability distribution must equal exactly 1.

quiz.q: If variance is 25, what is the standard deviation?

quiz.title: Permutations
quiz.description: Calculate permutations using nPr and factorial notation
quiz.formula:
Permutation Formula:
P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!

Factorial:
n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 2 × 1

Examples:
0! = 1, 1! = 1, 5! = 120

P(5, 3) = 5! / 2! = 60
P(n, n) = n!
quiz.content:
A permutation is an arrangement of objects where order matters. When selecting r objects from n distinct objects and arranging them in order, the number of permutations is P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!. For example, arranging 3 books from a collection of 5 gives P(5,3) = 60 different arrangements.

The factorial function n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n. Factorials grow extremely quickly: 10! = 3,628,800. A special case is 0! = 1. Permutations are used when every position is unique—like first, second, third place in a race, or creating PIN codes.
steps: Determine n (total number of objects available)
Determine r (number of positions to fill)
Apply the formula: P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!
Calculate the factorials in numerator and denominator
Simplify and compute the final answer

examples.title: Arranging Runners on a Podium
examples.text: 8 runners compete for gold, silver, bronze. P(8,3) = 8!/(8−3)! = 8!/5! = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 possible podium arrangements.

examples.title: Arranging All Letters
examples.text: How many ways to arrange 5 books on a shelf? P(5,5) = 5! = 120. When arranging all items, it is simply n!.

quiz.tip: Permutation means ORDER matters. If the question asks about presidents, rankings, passwords, or seating arrangements where position is important, use permutations. ABC and BAC are DIFFERENT permutations but the SAME combination.

quiz.q: P(6, 2) equals what?
How many 4-digit PIN codes can be made using digits 0–9 if no digit repeats?
What is the value of 0!?
quiz.explanation: By definition and mathematical convention, 0! = 1. This is necessary for permutation formulas to work correctly.

quiz.title: Combinations
quiz.description: Calculate combinations using nCr formula and understand when order matters vs doesn't
quiz.formula:
Combination Formula:
C(n, r) = n! / (r!(n − r)!)

Relationship to Permutations:
C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!

Examples:
C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! × 3!) = 10
C(10, 3) = 10! / (3! × 7!) = 120

Symmetry: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r)
quiz.content:
A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter. When choosing r objects from n distinct objects, the number of combinations is C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!). For example, choosing 2 friends from 5 gives C(5,2) = 10 different groups.

The key distinction: picking a president and vice-president is a permutation (ABC ≠ BAC). Picking 2 team captains is a combination (ABC = BAC). Combinations are always ≤ permutations for the same n and r, because C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r! accounts for all r! ways to rearrange the selection.
steps: Determine n (total objects) and r (objects being selected)
Decide: does order matter? If yes use P(n,r); if no use C(n,r)
Apply C(n,r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) or use Pascal's Triangle
Simplify by canceling common factors before multiplying
Check: C(n,r) should always equal C(n, n−r)

examples.title: Choosing a Committee
examples.text: From 7 people, choose 3 for a committee. C(7,3) = 7!/(3! × 4!) = (7×6×5)/(3×2×1) = 35. Order does not matter for committee members.

examples.title: Permutation vs Combination
examples.text: 5 people: choosing 2 for president and VP = P(5,2) = 20. Choosing 2 for a team = C(5,2) = 10. The permutation is 2! = 2 times larger.

quiz.tip: Ask yourself: 'If I swap two items, is it a different answer?' If yes — permutation. If no — combination. A pizza with pepperoni and mushroom is the same as one with mushroom and pepperoni!

quiz.q: C(8, 3) equals what?
Choosing 5 cards from a 52-card deck is a permutation or combination?
quiz.explanation: A poker hand has no inherent order, so it is a combination: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960 possible hands.

quiz.q: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r) is which property?
quiz.explanation: The symmetry property: choosing r items is the same as leaving behind n−r items. C(7,2) = C(7,5) = 21.

quiz.title: Vectors
quiz.description: Represent vectors as ordered pairs, find magnitude, add and subtract vectors
quiz.formula:
Component Form: v = ⟨x, y⟩

Magnitude:
|v| = √(x² + y²)

Vector Addition:
⟨a, b⟩ + ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a+c, b+d⟩

Scalar Multiplication:
k × ⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨kx, ky⟩

Unit Vector:
û = v/|v|
quiz.content:
A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction. Vectors are represented as ordered pairs ⟨x, y⟩, where x is the horizontal component and y is the vertical component. The magnitude is |v| = √(x² + y²).

Vector addition combines vectors by adding corresponding components. Geometrically, this follows the tip-to-tail method. Scalar multiplication stretches or shrinks a vector. A unit vector has magnitude 1 and points in the same direction as the original.
steps: Write the vector in component form ⟨x, y⟩
Find magnitude: |v| = √(x² + y²)
To add vectors: add corresponding x and y components
To subtract vectors: subtract corresponding x and y components
To find the unit vector: divide each component by the magnitude

examples.title: Finding Magnitude
examples.text: v = ⟨3, 4⟩. |v| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The vector has length 5 units.

examples.title: Vector Addition
examples.text: a = ⟨2, −1⟩, b = ⟨4, 3⟩. a + b = ⟨2+4, −1+3⟩ = ⟨6, 2⟩. The resultant goes 6 right and 2 up.

quiz.tip: Think of vectors as displacement: 'walk 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north.' The magnitude is the straight-line distance home (5 blocks), and the direction is the angle. Components are the east/west and north/south steps!

quiz.q: What is the magnitude of ⟨5, 12⟩?

quiz.explanation: Add components: 3 + (−1) = 2, 2 + 5 = 7. Result: ⟨2, 7⟩.

quiz.q: What is the unit vector of ⟨0, 1⟩?
quiz.explanation: |⟨0, 1⟩| = 1, so the unit vector is already ⟨0, 1⟩. It has magnitude 1!

quiz.title: Polar Coordinates
quiz.description: Convert between rectangular and polar coordinates and plot polar equations
quiz.formula:
Rectangular to Polar:
r = √(x² + y²)
θ = arctan(y/x)

Polar to Rectangular:
x = r cos(θ)
y = r sin(θ)

Note: Check quadrant when finding θ
Negative r: reflect through the origin
quiz.content:
Polar coordinates (r, θ) describe a point by its distance r from the origin (the pole) and the angle θ> measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis (polar axis). Unlike rectangular (x,y), polar uses distance and direction—like a radar screen.

To convert: x = r cos(θ) and y = r sin(θ) for polar to rectangular; r = √(x²+y²) with θ = arctan(y/x) for rectangular to polar. Be careful: arctan alone does not distinguish all quadrants. A negative r means go in the opposite direction: (−3, π/4) is the same as (3, 5π/4).
steps: To convert (x,y) to polar: find r = √(x² + y²)
Find θ = arctan(y/x) and adjust for the correct quadrant
To convert (r,θ) to rectangular: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ)
When plotting: rotate by θ from the polar axis, then move r units along that direction
Remember: (r,θ) and (−r, θ + π) represent the same point

examples.title: Rectangular to Polar
examples.text: Point (−3, 3). r = √(9+9) = 3√2. θ = arctan(3/(−3)) in Quadrant II: θ = 3π/4. Polar form: (3√2, 3π/4).

quiz.tip: Always sketch the point first! If a point is in Quadrant II (negative x, positive y), arctan gives a Quadrant IV angle—you must add π to correct it. Visualizing prevents quadrant errors.

quiz.q: Convert (2, 2) from rectangular to polar coordinates.
Convert (6, π) from polar to rectangular coordinates.
quiz.explanation: x = 6 cos(π) = 6(−1) = −6. y = 6 sin(π) = 0. Rectangular: (−6, 0).

quiz.q: Which point is the same as (2, π/3)?
quiz.explanation: (r,θ) = (−r, θ+π): (−2, π/3+π) = (−2, 4π/3) represents the same point.

quiz.title: Parametric Equations
quiz.description: Write and graph parametric equations, convert between parametric and rectangular
quiz.formula:
Parametric to Rectangular:
Given x = f(t), y = g(t),
solve for t in one equation
and substitute into the other.

Common Elimination:
x = r cos(t), y = r sin(t) → x² + y² = r² (circle)

Projectile:
x = v₀ cos(θ) × t
y = −½gt² + v₀ sin(θ) × t + h
quiz.content:
Parametric equations express x and y as functions of a parameter t. Instead of y = f(x), we write x = f(t) and y = g(t). This allows curves that fail the vertical line test and modeling motion over time.

To eliminate the parameter, solve one equation for t and substitute into the other. For example, if x = 2t and y = t²+1, then t = x/2 and y = (x/2)²+1 = x²/4+1. The orientation (direction of increasing t) matters—the same curve traced in opposite directions has different parametric equations.
steps: Identify the parametric equations x = f(t) and y = g(t)
Create a table of values by choosing t-values and computing x and y
Plot the (x, y) points to see the curve's shape
To eliminate: solve one equation for t, substitute into the other
Indicate orientation with arrows showing direction of increasing t

examples.title: Eliminating the Parameter
examples.text: x = 3 cos(t), y = 2 sin(t). Then (x/3)² + (y/2)² = cos²(t) + sin²(t) = 1. This is an ellipse: x²/9 + y²/4 = 1.

examples.title: Projectile Motion
examples.text: x = 50t, y = −16t² + 80t. Eliminate: t = x/50, y = −16(x/50)² + 80(x/50) = −16x²/2500 + 8x/5. A parabolic trajectory.

quiz.tip: When graphing parametric equations, always indicate direction with arrows. Two parametric equations might produce the same rectangular equation but trace the curve in different directions or at different speeds!

quiz.q: If x = t + 1 and y = t², what is the rectangular equation?
quiz.explanation: From x = t + 1, t = x − 1. Substitute: y = (x − 1)².

quiz.q: x = 4 cos(t), y = 4 sin(t) describes what shape?
quiz.explanation: x²/16 + y²/16 = 1, so x² + y² = 16, a circle of radius 4.

quiz.q: What does the parameter t represent in projectile motion?
quiz.explanation: In physics, t typically represents time, and x and y represent position at that time.

lessons.title: Piecewise Functions
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of piecewise functions
lessons.formula:
Piecewise notation:
        ⎧ a·x + b,   x < c
f(x) = ⎨ p·x² + q,   c ≤ x < d
        ⎩ r·x + s,    x ≥ d
Step function: f(x) = ⌊ x ⌋  (greatest integer ≤ x)
lessons.content:
A piecewise function is defined by different expressions over different intervals ("pieces") of its domain. Each sub-function applies only to a specific range of x-values, separated by conditional boundaries. The graph of a piecewise function may have distinct shapes on each interval.

When graphing, pay close attention to whether each boundary is included (closed dot, solid) or excluded (open dot, hollow). A closed dot means the endpoint satisfies ≤ or ≥; an open dot means the endpoint uses < or > and the value comes from the adjacent piece. Continuity occurs when the left-hand and right-hand limits match at each boundary.

Common piecewise functions include step functions (like the greatest integer function ⌊x⌋, which rounds down to the nearest integer), tax brackets, postage rates, and real-world pricing models. Evaluating a piecewise function means first determining which interval the input falls into, then applying the corresponding formula.
steps: Identify the domain intervals and their boundary values.
For each piece, graph the sub-function only on its specified interval.
Mark endpoints with closed dots (≤, ≥) or open dots (<, >).
Evaluate at a specific x by finding the correct interval first.
Check continuity: do the pieces connect at each boundary?

examples.title: Evaluate f(x) = { x² if x < 2; 2x + 1 if x ≥ 2 } at x = 1, 2, 3
examples.text: f(1): since 1 < 2, use f(x) = x² → f(1) = 1. f(2): since 2 ≥ 2, use f(x) = 2x + 1 → f(2) = 5. f(3): since 3 ≥ 2, use 2x + 1 → f(3) = 7. The function jumps from f(2⁻) = 4 to f(2) = 5, so it is discontinuous at x = 2.

examples.title: Greatest Integer Function: f(x) = ⌊x⌋
examples.text: f(3.7) = 3, f(-1.2) = -2, f(5) = 5. The graph is a series of horizontal steps, each one unit long, with open dots on the left and closed dots on the right. This is also called the floor function.

lessons.tip: When evaluating a piecewise function, always check the boundary condition first. If x equals a boundary value, use the interval that includes it (≤ or ≥). The other piece has an open dot there.

quiz.q: Given f(x) = { 3x + 1 if x < 0; x² if x ≥ 0 }, find f(-2) and f(0).
What does ⌊2.99⌋ equal?
quiz.explanation: The greatest integer function (floor) gives the greatest integer ≤ the value. The greatest integer ≤ 2.99 is 2.

quiz.q: At a boundary where the left piece has an open dot and the right piece has a closed dot, the function is:
quiz.explanation: The open dot means the left piece doesn't include that x-value, and the right piece does, creating a jump discontinuity.

quiz.q: A taxi charges $3 for the first mile and $2 for each additional mile. This is modeled by a:
quiz.explanation: The pricing changes at discrete boundaries (each mile), making it a piecewise or step function.

lessons.title: Composition of Functions
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of composition of functions
lessons.formula:
Composition:  (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))
Notation:     f(g(x))  or  (f ∘ g)(x)
Domain rule:  x must be in domain(g) AND g(x) must be in domain(f)
Decompose h(x):  if h(x) = √(3x + 1), then g(x) = 3x + 1, f(x) = √x
lessons.content:
Function composition means applying one function to the output of another. We write f(g(x)) or (f ∘ g)(x), which reads "f of g of x." Here, g(x) is the inner function (evaluated first) and f is the outer function (applied to the result). Note that (f ∘ g)(x) is generally NOT the same as (g ∘ f)(x).

To evaluate f(g(a)), first compute g(a), then substitute that result into f. When finding a general formula for (f ∘ g)(x), replace every x in f with the entire expression g(x). The domain of f ∘ g is the set of all x in the domain of g such that g(x) is also in the domain of f — this can be more restrictive than either domain alone.

Decomposition is the reverse process: given a composite function h(x), identify inner and outer functions. For example, h(x) = (2x + 3)² can be decomposed as f(u) = u² and g(x) = 2x + 3, so h = f ∘ g. This skill is essential for understanding the chain rule in calculus.
steps: Identify the inner function g(x) and outer function f(x).
Evaluate g(x) at the desired value of x.
Substitute g(x) into f in place of its variable.
Simplify the resulting expression.
Determine the domain: x must be in domain(g) and g(x) must be in domain(f).

examples.title: Find (f ∘ g)(x) where f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x²
examples.text: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x²) = 2(x²) + 1 = 2x² + 1. Compare with (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(2x+1) = (2x+1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1. The two compositions are clearly different.

lessons.tip: Composition order matters! f(g(x)) is NOT the same as g(f(x)). A helpful analogy: if f = 'put on socks' and g = 'put on shoes', then f(g(x)) = put on shoes then socks (wrong!), while g(f(x)) = put on socks then shoes (correct).

quiz.q: Given f(x) = 3x and g(x) = x + 5, find (f ∘ g)(2).
If f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = x - 3, find (g ∘ f)(x).
Decompose h(x) = √(5x - 7) into f ∘ g.
quiz.explanation: The outer function f acts on the inner result: f(u) = √u and g(x) = 5x - 7, so f(g(x)) = √(5x - 7).

quiz.q: The domain of f ∘ g is restricted by:
options: Both the domain of g and requiring g(x) to be in the domain of f
Neither; it is always all real numbers
quiz.explanation: x must be in domain(g), AND g(x) must produce a value that is in domain(f). Both conditions apply.

lessons.title: Inverse Functions
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of inverse functions
lessons.formula:
Finding an Inverse Function:
  1. Replace f(x) with y
  2. Swap x and y
  3. Solve for y
  4. Replace y with f⁻¹(x)

Verification:  f(f⁻¹(x)) = x  and  f⁻¹(f(x)) = x

Example:  f(x) = 2x + 3
  y = 2x + 3  →  x = 2y + 3  →  y = (x - 3)/2
  f⁻¹(x) = (x - 3)/2
lessons.content:
An inverse function undoes the action of the original function. If f maps an input x to an output y, then the inverse f⁻¹ maps y back to x. Not every function has an inverse — a function must be one-to-one (each output corresponds to exactly one input). You can test this with the horizontal line test: if any horizontal line crosses the graph more than once, the function is not invertible.

To find f⁻¹(x), replace f(x) with y, swap x and y, then solve the resulting equation for y. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y = x. For example, if f(x) = 2x + 3, swapping gives x = 2y + 3, so y = (x − 3)/2. Thus f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

Always verify your inverse by composing: f(f⁻¹(x)) should equal x. For f(x) = 2x + 3 and f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2, we get f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2·(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x − 3 + 3 = x. Some functions, like f(x) = x², are not one-to-one over all real numbers, so we restrict the domain (e.g., x ≥ 0) to create an invertible branch.
steps: Confirm the function is one-to-one using the horizontal line test
Write y = f(x), then interchange x and y in the equation
Solve the new equation for y using algebraic techniques
Replace y with f⁻¹(x) to denote the inverse function
Verify by computing f(f⁻¹(x)) and confirming it equals x

examples.title: Finding the Inverse of f(x) = (3x + 1) / 5
examples.text:
Step 1: y = (3x + 1) / 5
Step 2: Swap: x = (3y + 1) / 5
Step 3: Multiply both sides by 5: 5x = 3y + 1
Step 4: Subtract 1: 5x − 1 = 3y
Step 5: Divide by 3: y = (5x − 1) / 3
So f⁻¹(x) = (5x − 1) / 3. Check: f(f⁻¹(2)) = f(3) = (9+1)/5 = 2. ✓

examples.title: Domain Restriction: f(x) = x², x ≥ 0
examples.text: The full parabola y = x² fails the horizontal line test, so we restrict to x ≥ 0 (the right half). Swapping gives x = y², so y = √x. Thus f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0 and range y ≥ 0. Verification: f(f⁻¹(9)) = f(3) = 3² = 9. ✓

lessons.tip: When finding an inverse, always verify with BOTH compositions: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x AND f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. If either fails, check your algebra — a common mistake is forgetting to swap x and y before solving.

quiz.q: What is the inverse of f(x) = 4x − 7?
quiz.explanation: Swap x and y: x = 4y − 7. Solve: x + 7 = 4y, so y = (x + 7)/4.

quiz.q: Which function fails the horizontal line test and therefore has no inverse without restricting the domain?
quiz.explanation: f(x) = |x| maps both 3 and −3 to 3, so a horizontal line at y = 3 hits twice. The domain must be restricted (e.g., x ≥ 0) for an inverse.

quiz.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(f⁻¹(5))?
quiz.explanation: By definition, f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for all x in the domain. So f(f⁻¹(5)) = 5.

quiz.q: The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the original graph across which line?
quiz.explanation: The inverse function's graph is the mirror image of f across the line y = x.

lessons.title: Solving Quadratics by Completing the Square
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of solving quadratics by completing the square
lessons.formula:
Completing the Square for ax² + bx + c = 0:

1. Divide by a (if a ≠ 1):  x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0
2. Move constant:  x² + (b/a)x = −c/a
3. Add (b/2a)² to both sides:
   x² + (b/a)x + (b/2a)² = (b/2a)² − c/a
4. Factor: (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac) / 4a²

Vertex form: f(x) = a(x − h)² + k
Vertex: (h, k) where h = −b/(2a)
lessons.content:
Completing the square is an algebraic technique that rewrites a quadratic expression ax² + bx + c into vertex form a(x − h)² + k, which reveals the parabola's vertex at (h, k). The key idea is to add a specific constant to form a perfect square trinomial, which factors cleanly as (x + p)².

To complete the square on x² + bx, take half of the coefficient of x (that is, b/2), square it to get (b/2)², and add it to both sides of the equation. For example, x² + 6x becomes (x + 3)² − 9 because (6/2)² = 9. This technique also derives the quadratic formula and is essential for converting to vertex form for graphing parabolas.

When the leading coefficient a is not 1, first factor it out before completing the square. For instance, to solve 2x² − 12x + 10 = 0, factor out 2 to get 2(x² − 6x) + 10 = 0, then 2(x² − 6x + 9) + 10 = 18, simplifying to 2(x − 3)² = 8, giving x − 3 = ±2, so x = 1 or x = 5.
steps: Ensure the coefficient of x² is 1 (divide all terms by a if necessary)
Move the constant term to the right side of the equation
Take half of the coefficient of x, square it, and add to both sides
Factor the left side as a perfect square trinomial (x + b/2)²
Take the square root of both sides and solve for x (remember ±)

examples.title: Solve x² + 8x − 5 = 0 by completing the square
Convert f(x) = 3x² + 12x + 7 to vertex form
examples.text:
Factor out 3: f(x) = 3(x² + 4x) + 7
Half of 4 is 2, and 2² = 4. Add inside and compensate:
f(x) = 3(x² + 4x + 4) + 7 − 12
f(x) = 3(x + 2)² − 5
Vertex is (−2, −5). The parabola opens upward with axis of symmetry x = −2.

lessons.tip: Completing the square always works, even when the quadratic doesn't factor nicely. It's also the technique used to derive the quadratic formula, so understanding it deeply gives you insight into why the formula looks the way it does.

quiz.q: What do you add to x² + 10x to complete the square?
quiz.explanation: Half of 10 is 5, and 5² = 25. So x² + 10x + 25 = (x + 5)².

quiz.q: Solve (x − 3)² = 16. What are the solutions?
What is the vertex of f(x) = −2(x + 1)² + 9?
quiz.explanation: In vertex form f(x) = a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h, k). Here h = −1 and k = 9.

quiz.q: To complete the square on 3x² + 18x, what should you do first?
quiz.explanation: When the leading coefficient isn't 1, always factor it out first: 3(x² + 6x), then complete the square on the expression inside the parentheses.

lessons.title: Quadratic Formula & the Discriminant
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of quadratic formula & the discriminant
lessons.formula:
Quadratic Formula (for ax² + bx + c = 0):

        x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a

Discriminant:  Δ = b² − 4ac

If Δ > 0  →  Two distinct real roots
If Δ = 0  →  One repeated real root
If Δ < 0  →  Two complex conjugate roots

Axis of symmetry:  x = −b / 2a
Vertex x-coordinate:  h = −b / 2a
lessons.content:
The quadratic formula gives the solutions to any quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, regardless of whether it factors. The formula is derived by completing the square on the general form and works for all real coefficients a, b, c where a ≠ 0. The expression under the radical, b² − 4ac, is called the discriminant (Δ) and tells you the nature of the roots.

If Δ > 0, the equation has two distinct real solutions; if Δ = 0, there is exactly one repeated real root (the parabola touches the x-axis at its vertex); if Δ < 0, the roots are complex conjugates of the form p ± qi. For example, 2x² − 6x + 5 = 0 has Δ = 36 − 40 = −4, giving x = (6 ± 2i) / 4 = 1.5 ± 0.5i.

The discriminant also connects to graphing: Δ > 0 means the parabola crosses the x-axis twice, Δ = 0 means it's tangent to the x-axis, and Δ < 0 means the parabola never touches the x-axis. The axis of symmetry of the parabola is always x = −b/(2a), which is also the x-coordinate of the vertex.
steps: Write the equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0
Identify coefficients a, b, and c (watch for signs!)
Calculate the discriminant: Δ = b² − 4ac
Evaluate the nature of roots from Δ (positive, zero, or negative)
Substitute a, b, and Δ into the quadratic formula and simplify

examples.title: Find the discriminant and classify roots of x² + 4x + 13 = 0

lessons.tip: Always compute the discriminant FIRST before substituting into the full formula. This saves time — if Δ = 0, you know there's only one root (x = −b/2a) and can skip the ± calculation. Also, keep values exact (in radical form) until the final answer to avoid rounding errors.

quiz.q: For 2x² + 3x − 2 = 0, what is the discriminant?
If the discriminant is negative, which statement is true?
options: There are two distinct real roots
There are two complex conjugate roots
quiz.explanation: A negative discriminant means the parabola doesn't cross the x-axis. The solutions are complex numbers of the form p ± qi.

quiz.q: The axis of symmetry of the parabola 4x² − 8x + 1 is:
quiz.explanation: Axis of symmetry is x = −b/(2a) = −(−8)/(2·4) = 8/8 = 1.

quiz.q: If Δ = 0 for ax² + bx + c = 0, how many x-intercepts does the parabola have?
quiz.explanation: Δ = 0 means the parabola touches the x-axis at exactly one point (the vertex), giving one repeated root.

lessons.title: Complex Number Operations
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of complex number operations
lessons.formula:
Complex Number:  z = a + bi, where i² = −1

Addition:    (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i
Subtraction: (a + bi) − (c + di) = (a − c) + (b − d)i
Multiplication:
  (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i

Division (multiply by conjugate):
  (a + bi) / (c + di) = [(a + bi)(c − di)] / (c² + d²)

Modulus: |z| = √(a² + b²)
Conjugate: z̄ = a − bi
lessons.content:
A complex number is written as a + bi, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part. The imaginary unit i is defined as i = √(−1), so i² = −1. Complex numbers extend the real number line into the complex plane, where the horizontal axis represents the real part and the vertical axis represents the imaginary part.

Adding and subtracting complex numbers is straightforward: combine real parts with real parts, and imaginary parts with imaginary parts. For multiplication, use the distributive property (FOIL) and replace i² with −1. For example, (3 + 2i)(1 − 4i) = 3 − 12i + 2i − 8i² = 3 − 10i + 8 = 11 − 10i. Division requires multiplying the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator.

The complex conjugate of a + bi is a − bi, and multiplying a complex number by its conjugate always yields a real number: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b². The modulus (distance from the origin) of z = a + bi is |z| = √(a² + b²). These operations are essential for solving quadratics with negative discriminants and for advanced topics in engineering and physics.
steps: Identify the real part (a) and imaginary part (b) of each complex number
For addition/subtraction: combine like terms (real with real, imaginary with imaginary)
For multiplication: use FOIL and simplify i² to −1
For division: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator
Simplify the result by combining real and imaginary terms

examples.title: Divide (6 + 2i) / (3 − i)
examples.text:
Multiply top and bottom by conjugate (3 + i):
= [(6 + 2i)(3 + i)] / [(3 − i)(3 + i)]
Numerator: 18 + 6i + 6i + 2i² = 18 + 12i − 2 = 16 + 12i
Denominator: 3² − (i)² = 9 − (−1) = 10
= (16 + 12i) / 10 = 8/5 + (6/5)i

lessons.tip: When multiplying complex numbers, always remember that i² = −1. A common mistake is forgetting to convert i² terms. Also, for division problems, the denominator always becomes a real number after multiplying by the conjugate, since (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².

quiz.q: What is (5 + 3i) + (2 − 7i)?
quiz.explanation: Combine real parts: 5 + 2 = 7. Combine imaginary parts: 3i + (−7i) = −4i. Result: 7 − 4i.

quiz.q: Simplify i⁻¹⁸ (i to the 18th power).
quiz.explanation: Powers of i cycle every 4: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Since 18 ÷ 4 = 4 remainder 2, i¹⁸ = i² = −1.

quiz.q: What is the complex conjugate of 7 − 3i?
quiz.explanation: The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. So the conjugate of 7 + (−3)i = 7 − 3i is 7 − (−3)i = 7 + 3i.

quiz.q: What is the modulus of 3 + 4i?

lessons.title: Polynomial Graphs & End Behavior
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of polynomial graphs & end behavior
lessons.formula:
End Behavior Rules:

Even degree, positive leading coeff:
  Both ends rise  →  ∞ as x → ±∞

Even degree, negative leading coeff:
  Both ends fall  →  −∞ as x → ±∞

Odd degree, positive leading coeff:
  Falls left, rises right

Odd degree, negative leading coeff:
  Rises left, falls right

Maximum turning points = degree − 1
Maximum x-intercepts = degree
lessons.content:
The end behavior of a polynomial describes what happens to f(x) as x approaches positive or negative infinity. It is determined by two factors: the degree (highest power of x) and the leading coefficient (the coefficient of the highest-degree term). Even-degree polynomials have both ends going the same direction, while odd-degree polynomials have ends going in opposite directions.

For example, f(x) = 2x⁴ − 3x³ + x − 5 has even degree (4) and a positive leading coefficient (2), so both ends of the graph rise toward +∞. In contrast, g(x) = −3x³ + x² − 4 has odd degree (3) and negative leading coefficient, so the left end rises and the right end falls.

The multiplicity of a zero affects how the graph behaves at each x-intercept. A zero of odd multiplicity causes the graph to cross the x-axis; a zero of even multiplicity causes it to touch and bounce off. A polynomial of degree n can have at most n − 1 turning points (local maxima and minima) and at most n x-intercepts.
steps: Identify the degree (highest exponent) and leading coefficient of the polynomial
Determine end behavior using the degree (even/odd) and sign of the leading coefficient
Find the x-intercepts by setting the polynomial equal to zero and factoring
Determine the y-intercept by evaluating f(0)
Identify turning points and sketch the graph, noting multiplicity at each zero

examples.title: Describe the end behavior of f(x) = −2x⁵ + 7x³ − x
examples.text:
Degree is 5 (odd), leading coefficient is −2 (negative).
Odd degree + negative leading coeff: rises to the left, falls to the right.
As x → −∞, f(x) → +∞  (left end goes up)
As x → +∞, f(x) → −∞  (right end goes down)
Maximum turning points: 5 − 1 = 4

examples.title: Graph behavior of f(x) = x²(x − 3)²(x + 1)
examples.text:
Expand the leading term: the highest power is x² · x² · x = x⁵ (odd degree, positive coeff).
End behavior: falls left, rises right.
Zeros: x = 0 (mult. 2, touches), x = 3 (mult. 2, touches), x = −1 (mult. 1, crosses).
Max turning points: 5 − 1 = 4. The graph crosses at x = −1 but bounces at x = 0 and x = 3.

lessons.tip: A quick trick for end behavior: just look at the leading term axⁿ. If n is even, both ends match the sign of a. If n is odd, the left end is opposite to the sign of a. You can ignore all lower-degree terms when determining end behavior.

quiz.q: What is the end behavior of f(x) = 5x⁶ − 2x + 1?
quiz.explanation: Degree 6 is even, leading coefficient 5 is positive. Even degree + positive coeff = both ends rise.

quiz.q: A polynomial of degree 7 can have at most how many turning points?
quiz.explanation: A polynomial of degree n has at most n − 1 turning points. So 7 − 1 = 6.

quiz.q: If f(x) = (x + 2)³(x − 1), what happens at x = −2?
options: The graph bounces off the x-axis
The graph crosses the x-axis with a flattened shape
The graph has a vertical asymptote
quiz.explanation: x = −2 has odd multiplicity (3), so the graph crosses. Because the multiplicity is greater than 1, the crossing appears flattened.

quiz.q: The end behavior of −4x³ + 10x is:
quiz.explanation: Degree 3 is odd, leading coefficient −4 is negative. Odd + negative = rises to the left, falls to the right.

lessons.title: Factoring Higher-Degree Polynomials
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of factoring higher-degree polynomials
lessons.formula:
Special Factoring Patterns:

Difference of Squares:  a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)
Sum of Cubes:  a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
Difference of Cubes:  a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)

Rational Root Theorem:
  Possible rational roots = ±(p/q)
  where p = factors of constant term
  and q = factors of leading coefficient

Factor Theorem: If f(r) = 0, then (x − r) is a factor.
lessons.content:
Factoring higher-degree polynomials (degree 3 and above) requires a systematic strategy. First, always look for a greatest common factor (GCF) among all terms. Then check for special patterns: difference of squares (a² − b²), sum of cubes (a³ + b³), or difference of cubes (a³ − b³). For four-term polynomials, factoring by grouping pairs terms to reveal a common binomial factor.

When special patterns don't apply, use the Rational Root Theorem to list all possible rational roots as ±factors of the constant / factors of the leading coefficient. Test these candidates by evaluating f(r) — if f(r) = 0, then (x − r) is a factor (Factor Theorem). Once you find one root, use synthetic division to reduce the polynomial to a lower degree and repeat.

For example, to factor x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, possible rational roots are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6. Testing f(1) = 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor. Synthetic division by (x − 1) gives x² − 5x + 6, which factors to (x − 2)(x − 3). Full factorization: (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).
steps: Factor out the GCF from all terms first
Check for special factoring patterns (difference of squares, sum/difference of cubes)
List all possible rational roots using the Rational Root Theorem
Test candidates until you find a root r where f(r) = 0
Use synthetic division to factor out (x − r), then factor the remaining quotient

examples.title: Factor x³ + 8 using the sum of cubes formula
examples.text:
x³ + 8 = x³ + 2³
Sum of cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
Here a = x, b = 2:
x³ + 8 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4)
The quadratic x² − 2x + 4 has discriminant 4 − 16 = −12, so it doesn't factor further over the reals.

examples.title: Factor 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6 completely
examples.text:
Possible rational roots: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, ±1/2, ±3/2
Test f(3): 2(27) − 3(9) − 11(3) + 6 = 54 − 27 − 33 + 6 = 0. ✓
Synthetic division by (x − 3):
  2  −3  −11   6  |  3
     6    9  −6
  2   3   −2   0
Quotient: 2x² + 3x − 2 = (2x − 1)(x + 2)
Full factorization: (x − 3)(2x − 1)(x + 2)

lessons.tip: When testing rational roots, start with the smallest integers (±1, ±2) before trying larger values or fractions. Also, use Descartes' Rule of Signs to predict the number of positive and negative real roots — this narrows your list of candidates significantly.

quiz.q: Factor x³ − 27 completely.
quiz.explanation: x³ − 27 = x³ − 3³ = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9) by the difference of cubes formula.

quiz.q: According to the Rational Root Theorem, which is a possible rational root of 6x³ + x² − 10x + 3 = 0?
quiz.explanation: Possible rational roots = ±(factors of 3)/(factors of 6) = ±1, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2, ±1/3, ±1/6. Among the options, 1/2 is valid since 1 divides 3 and 2 divides 6. The others (5, 2/5, 1/5) are invalid because 5 does not divide 3.

quiz.q: Factor 4x³ − 16x by first taking out the GCF.
quiz.explanation: GCF is 4x: 4x(x² − 4) = 4x(x + 2)(x − 2) using difference of squares.

quiz.q: If f(−2) = 0 for a polynomial f(x), which must be true?
quiz.explanation: By the Factor Theorem, if f(r) = 0, then (x − r) is a factor. Since r = −2, the factor is (x − (−2)) = (x + 2).

lessons.title: Rational Inequalities
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of rational inequalities
lessons.formula:
Solving Rational Inequalities:

1. Move all terms to one side (zero on the other)
2. Combine into a single fraction: P(x)/Q(x) > 0 (or <, ≥, ≤)
3. Find critical values:
   - Zeros of numerator (where expression = 0)
   - Zeros of denominator (where expression is undefined)
4. Test a value in each interval on the sign chart
5. Select intervals matching the inequality

Key rule: DENOMINATOR ZEROS ARE ALWAYS EXCLUDED
(≥/≤: numerator zeros ARE included)
lessons.content:
A rational inequality involves a fraction of two polynomials set in a relationship with zero, such as (x − 2)/(x + 3) > 0. Unlike rational equations, where you cross-multiply, solving inequalities requires tracking the sign of the expression across different intervals. The boundary points where the numerator or denominator equals zero are called critical values and divide the number line into regions of consistent sign.

The test interval method (or sign chart method) is the standard approach. After combining all terms into a single fraction, find all critical values. For a strict inequality (< or >), both numerator zeros and denominator zeros create open boundaries (excluded). For a non-strict inequality (≤ or ≥), numerator zeros are included (closed boundary) but denominator zeros are always excluded because division by zero is undefined.

For example, to solve (x + 1)(x − 4)/(x + 2) ≤ 0, the critical values are x = −1 (numerator zero, included), x = 4 (numerator zero, included), and x = −2 (denominator zero, excluded). Testing intervals reveals the solution is [−2, −1] ∪ [0, 4]. The key principle: a rational expression changes sign only at critical values.
steps: Rewrite the inequality so one side is zero and the other is a single rational expression
Factor the numerator and denominator completely to find all critical values
Mark critical values on a number line (open circles for excluded, closed for included)
Test a value from each interval to determine whether the expression is positive or negative
Select the intervals that satisfy the inequality and write the solution

examples.title: Solve (x − 3) / (x + 1) > 0
examples.text:
Critical values: x = 3 (numerator = 0), x = −1 (denominator = 0, excluded)

Test intervals:
(-∞, −1): test x = −2: (−5)/(−1) = 5 > 0 ✓
(−1, 3):  test x = 0: (−3)/(1) = −3 < 0  ✗
(3, ∞):    test x = 4: (1)/(5) = 0.2 > 0 ✓

Solution: (-∞, −1) ∪ (3, ∞)

lessons.tip: NEVER multiply both sides of a rational inequality by the denominator — you don't know if it's positive or negative, which would flip the inequality sign. Always move everything to one side and use the sign chart method instead. It's safer and works every time.

quiz.q: When solving (x + 5) / (x − 2) < 0, what happens at x = 2?
options: It is included in the solution
It is excluded because the expression is undefined there
quiz.explanation: x = 2 makes the denominator zero, so the expression is undefined. It must always be excluded from the solution set.

quiz.q: The solution to (x − 1)(x + 4) / (x − 3) ≥ 0 includes which of these values?
quiz.explanation: x = −4 makes the numerator zero, and since ≥ allows equality, it's included. x = 3 is excluded (denominator zero).

quiz.q: How many test intervals do you need for (x² − 9)(x + 1) / (x − 5) < 0?
quiz.explanation: The critical values are x = −3, x = −1, x = 3 (numerator zeros) and x = 5 (denominator zero). Four critical values divide the number line into 5 intervals: (−∞, −3), (−3, −1), (−1, 3), (3, 5), and (5, ∞).

quiz.q: Why can't you cross-multiply when solving rational inequalities?
options: The denominator's sign is unknown, so multiplying could flip the inequality the wrong way
quiz.explanation: Cross-multiplying is valid for equations (=), but for inequalities, you'd need to know whether the denominator is positive or negative to decide whether to flip the sign. Since it varies, always use the sign chart method.

lessons.title: Exponential Growth & Decay
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of exponential growth & decay
lessons.formula:
Exponential Growth:  A(t) = A₀(1 + r)ᵗ
  A₀ = initial amount, r = growth rate, t = time

Exponential Decay:  A(t) = A₀(1 − r)ᵗ

Continuous Compounding:
  A(t) = A₀ · eˣ⁴

Half-life formula:  A(t) = A₀(1/2)^(t/h)
  h = half-life

Doubling time:  t_d = ln(2) / ln(1 + r)
Half-life from rate:  h = −ln(2) / ln(1 − r)

Note: e ≈ 2.71828
lessons.content:
Exponential growth and decay describe situations where a quantity increases or decreases by a constant percentage per time period, rather than a constant amount. In exponential growth, the quantity grows proportionally to its current size — the bigger it gets, the faster it grows. Common examples include population growth, compound interest, and bacterial reproduction. Exponential decay occurs in radioactive decay, drug elimination from the body, and depreciation.

The general form is A(t) = A₀ · bᵗ, where A₀ is the initial amount, b is the growth factor (b > 1 for growth, 0 < b < 1 for decay), and t is time. For growth, b = 1 + r where r is the rate as a decimal. For decay, b = 1 − r. When growth occurs continuously, we use the natural exponential: A(t) = A₀ · eˣ⁴, where e ≈ 2.718.

Half-life is the time required for a decaying quantity to reduce to half its initial value. For example, carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, meaning after 5,730 years only 50% of the original amount remains. The doubling time in growth can be found using t_d = ln(2)/ln(1 + r). All exponential functions have a horizontal asymptote at y = 0 (for decay, the value approaches 0 but never reaches it).
steps: Identify whether the situation represents growth (b > 1) or decay (0 < b < 1)
Determine the initial value A₀, the rate r, and the time unit
Write the exponential function: A(t) = A₀(1 + r)ᵗ for growth or A(t) = A₀(1 − r)ᵗ for decay
Substitute the given values to find the unknown quantity
Interpret the result in context (e.g., "after 10 years, the population will be...")

examples.title: A bacteria culture doubles every 3 hours. If the initial population is 500, find the population after 12 hours.
examples.text:
Growth factor per 3 hours: b = 2 (doubles)
Number of 3-hour periods in 12 hours: t = 12/3 = 4
A(4) = 500 · 2⁴ = 500 · 16 = 8,000
After 12 hours, the population is 8,000 bacteria.

Using continuous model: A = 500 · e^(ln(2) · 12/3) = 500 · e^(2.773) ≈ 8,000

examples.title: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 days. If you start with 160 grams, how much remains after 24 days?

lessons.tip: To distinguish exponential from linear growth, check if the ratio between successive values is constant (exponential) or the difference is constant (linear). If a table shows y-values of 3, 6, 12, 24, the ratio is always 2 (exponential). If it shows 3, 6, 9, 12, the difference is always 3 (linear).

quiz.q: A population of 1,000 grows at 5% per year. What is the population after 3 years?
The half-life of radon-222 is 3.8 days. If you start with 80 mg, how much remains after 11.4 days?
quiz.explanation: 11.4 / 3.8 = 3 half-lives. After 3 half-lives: 80 × (1/2)³ = 80 × 1/8 = 10 mg.

quiz.q: In the formula A(t) = A₀ · e^(0.08t), what does 0.08 represent?
quiz.explanation: In A(t) = A₀ · e^(kt), the value k is the continuous growth rate. Here k = 0.08, meaning 8% continuous growth.

quiz.q: Which function represents exponential decay?
quiz.explanation: Exponential decay has a base between 0 and 1. Here 0.75 < 1, so f(x) = 3(0.75)ˣ decays over time.

lessons.title: Logarithm Properties & Equations
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of logarithm properties & equations
lessons.formula:
Product Rule:  log_b(MN) = log_b(M) + log_b(N)
Quotient Rule: log_b(M/N) = log_b(M) − log_b(N)
Power Rule: log_b(M^p) = p · log_b(M)
Change of Base: log_b(x) = ln(x) / ln(b)
Logarithm → Exponential: log_b(x) = y  ⟺  b^y = x
lessons.content:
Logarithms are the inverse operations of exponentials. The expression log_b(x) = y means “the base b raised to what power gives x?” For example, log_2(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8. The product rule states that log_b(MN) = log_b(M) + log_b(N), the quotient rule gives log_b(M/N) = log_b(M) − log_b(N), and the power rule lets you pull an exponent out front: log_b(M^p) = p · log_b(M). These three rules are used together to expand or condense logarithmic expressions.

Solving a logarithmic equation usually involves rewriting it in exponential form or condensing multiple logs into a single logarithm using the properties. For instance, to solve log_3(x) + log_3(x − 2) = 1, combine the left side with the product rule to get log_3(x(x − 2)) = 1, then rewrite as 3¹ = x² − 2x, yielding the quadratic x² − 2x − 3 = 0 with solutions x = 3 (valid) and x = −1 (rejected because log_3(−1) is undefined).

The change-of-base formula, log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b), lets you evaluate logarithms with any base on a calculator that only has common log (base 10) and natural log (base e) keys. In real-world applications, the Richter scale for earthquakes and the pH scale for acidity are both logarithmic: a pH of 4 is ten times more acidic than a pH of 5 because pH = −log₁₀[H⁺].
steps: Identify which logarithm property (product, quotient, power) applies to each part of the expression
Expand a single log into a sum or difference of logs, or condense multiple logs into one
Rewrite the logarithmic equation in exponential form: log_b(x) = y becomes b^y = x
Solve the resulting algebraic equation and check every solution in the original log expression
Reject any solution that produces a non-positive argument inside a logarithm (domain restriction)

examples.title: Expanding a Logarithmic Expression
examples.text:
Expand log_3(27x⁴ / y²) completely.

Step 1: Apply the quotient rule: log_3(27x⁴) − log_3(y²).
Step 2: Apply the product rule to the first term: log_3(27) + log_3(x⁴) − log_3(y²).
Step 3: Evaluate log_3(27) = 3 (since 3³ = 27) and apply the power rule: 3 + 4·log_3(x) − 2·log_3(y).

Final answer: 3 + 4·log_3(x) − 2·log_3(y)

examples.title: Solving a Logarithmic Equation
examples.text:
Solve log_2(x + 1) + log_2(x − 1) = 3.

Step 1: Condense using the product rule: log_2((x+1)(x−1)) = 3.
Step 2: Rewrite in exponential form: (x+1)(x−1) = 2³ = 8.
Step 3: Expand: x² − 1 = 8, so x² = 9, giving x = 3 or x = −3.
Step 4: Check domain: x + 1 > 0 and x − 1 > 0, so x > 1.
Step 5: x = 3 is valid; x = −3 is rejected.

Solution: x = 3

lessons.tip: Always check the domain of every logarithm BEFORE solving. If log_b(arg) appears, then arg > 0. Solutions that violate this are extraneous.

quiz.q: Using the product rule, log_4(8) + log_4(2) equals:
quiz.explanation: Product rule: log_4(8·2) = log_4(16) = 2, because 4² = 16.

quiz.q: Evaluate log_3(81) without a calculator:
Solve log_5(x) = 2 for x:
quiz.explanation: Rewrite as 5² = x, so x = 25.

quiz.q: Which expression is equivalent to 2·log_7(x)?
quiz.explanation: The power rule gives p·log_b(M) = log_b(M^p), so 2·log_7(x) = log_7(x²).

lessons.title: Arithmetic & Geometric Sequences/Series
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of arithmetic & geometric sequences/series
lessons.formula:
Arithmetic nth term: a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d
Arithmetic series sum: S_n = n/2 · (a₁ + a_n) = n/2 · [2a₁ + (n−1)d]
Geometric nth term: a_n = a₁ · r^(n−1)
Geometric series sum: S_n = a₁(1 − r^n) / (1 − r),  r ≠ 1
Infinite geometric sum: S_∞ = a₁ / (1 − r),  |r| < 1
lessons.content:
An arithmetic sequence adds a constant common difference d to each term: 3, 7, 11, 15, … has d = 4. The n-th term is a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d. A geometric sequence multiplies each term by a constant common ratio r: 2, 6, 18, 54, … has r = 3. The n-th term is a_n = a₁ · rn−1.

A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence. The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic series is Sn = n/2 · (a₁ + an). For a geometric series, Sn = a₁(1 − rn) / (1 − r). When |r| < 1, the infinite geometric series converges to S∞ = a₁ / (1 − r). For example, 0.333… = 3/10 + 3/100 + 3/1000 + … with a₁ = 0.3 and r = 0.1, giving S∞ = 0.3 / (1 − 0.1) = 1/3.

Sequences and series appear throughout mathematics and science: compound interest is a geometric sequence, amortization schedules use arithmetic series, and fractal geometry relies on infinite geometric series to compute dimensions and areas.
steps: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic (constant difference) or geometric (constant ratio)
Find the common difference d or common ratio r by subtracting or dividing consecutive terms
Use the appropriate n-th term formula to find any specific term a_n
For a series sum, identify n (number of terms), then apply the correct sum formula
For infinite series, verify |r| < 1 before using S_∞ = a₁ / (1 − r)

examples.title: Sum of an Arithmetic Series
examples.text:
Find the sum of the first 20 terms of: 5, 11, 17, 23, …

Step 1: Common difference d = 11 − 5 = 6.
Step 2: a₁ = 5, n = 20.
Step 3: a₂₀ = 5 + (20 − 1)(6) = 5 + 114 = 119.
Step 4: S₂₀ = (20/2)(5 + 119) = 10 × 124 = 1,240.

Answer: S₂₀ = 1,240

examples.title: Sum of an Infinite Geometric Series
examples.text:
Evaluate 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 + …

Step 1: a₁ = 8, r = 4/8 = 0.5.
Step 2: Check convergence: |0.5| < 1, so the series converges.
Step 3: S_∞ = 8 / (1 − 0.5) = 8 / 0.5 = 16.

Answer: The sum is 16.

lessons.tip: To find the number of terms in an arithmetic series, solve n from a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d first, then plug n into the sum formula.

quiz.q: In the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, …, what is the 50th term?
What is the common ratio of 5, −10, 20, −40, …?
Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 2, 6, 18, 54, …:
Does the infinite geometric series 1 + 1.1 + 1.21 + 1.331 + … converge?
options: Yes, because the terms are positive
No, because there is no common ratio
quiz.explanation: r = 1.1 and |1.1| ≥ 1, so the infinite geometric series does not converge.

lessons.title: The Unit Circle
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of the unit circle
lessons.formula:
Definition: x² + y² = 1  (unit circle equation)
cos θ = x-coordinate,  sin θ = y-coordinate
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = y / x
Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
Radians ↔ Degrees: 180° = π radians
lessons.content:
The unit circle is a circle centered at the origin with radius 1. Every point on the circle satisfies x² + y² = 1. When a ray from the origin makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, the coordinates of the intersection point are (cos θ, sin θ). This single fact gives you the values of sine and cosine for every angle.

Special angles at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° (and their multiples) have exact trigonometric values worth memorizing. For example, at 60° (π/3), the coordinates are (1/2, √3/2), so cos 60° = 1/2 and sin 60° = √3/2. A reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis; in Quadrant II the reference angle for 120° is 60°, and the signs of sin and cos depend on the quadrant (All Students Take Calculus: All positive in QI, Sine in QII, Tangent in QIII, Cosine in QIV).

Radian measure is the arc length subtended by the angle on the unit circle. A full revolution is 2π radians = 360°, so π radians = 180° and π/2 = 90°. Radians are the preferred unit in calculus because derivative formulas for trigonometric functions assume the argument is in radians.
steps: Draw the unit circle and mark the quadrant of the given angle
Find the reference angle: for θ in QII use 180°−θ, in QIII use θ−180°, in QIV use 360°−θ
Determine the (cos, sin) coordinates of the reference angle from the special angle values
Apply the correct sign based on the quadrant: QI (+,+), QII (−,+), QIII (−,−), QIV (+,−)
If the angle is in radians, verify by converting: multiply degrees by π/180 or radians by 180/π

examples.title: Finding Coordinates on the Unit Circle
examples.text:
Find (cos 150°, sin 150°).

Step 1: 150° is in Quadrant II.
Step 2: Reference angle = 180° − 150° = 30°.
Step 3: At 30°, coordinates are (√3/2, 1/2).
Step 4: In QII, cosine is negative and sine is positive.

Answer: cos 150° = −√3/2, sin 150° = 1/2.

examples.title: Converting Between Degrees and Radians
examples.text:
Convert 5π/4 radians to degrees and find its reference angle.

Step 1: Multiply by 180/π: (5π/4)(180/π) = 225°.
Step 2: 225° is in Quadrant III.
Step 3: Reference angle = 225° − 180° = 45°.

Answer: 225° with reference angle 45° (so |cos| = |sin| = √2/2, both negative in QIII).

lessons.tip: Memorize the coordinates for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° in the first quadrant, then use reference angles and quadrant signs to derive all other special values.

quiz.q: What are the coordinates (cos θ, sin θ) at θ = 45°?
quiz.explanation: At 45° on the unit circle, x = y = √2/2 ≈ 0.707.

quiz.q: In which quadrant is sin θ positive and cos θ negative?
quiz.explanation: In QII, x < 0 (cos negative) and y > 0 (sin positive).

What is tan(π/4)?

lessons.title: Trigonometric Graphs
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of trigonometric graphs
lessons.formula:
General sine: y = A·sin(B(x − C)) + D
General cosine: y = A·cos(B(x − C)) + D
Amplitude = |A|
Period = 2π / |B|
Phase shift = C
Midline (vertical shift) = D
lessons.content:
The graphs of sine and cosine are smooth, repeating waves called sinusoidal functions. The basic graph of y = sin(x) starts at the origin, rises to a maximum of 1 at x = π/2, returns to 0 at x = π, reaches a minimum of −1 at x = 3π/2, and completes one full cycle at x = 2π. The basic graph of y = cos(x) starts at a maximum of 1 and has the same period.

Transformations modify these basic graphs in predictable ways. The amplitude |A| stretches or compresses the wave vertically. The period is 2π/|B|; larger B values produce shorter periods (faster oscillation). The phase shift C moves the graph left (if C > 0) or right (if C < 0). The vertical shift D moves the midline up or down. For example, y = 3 sin(2x − π) + 1 has amplitude 3, period π, phase shift π/2 to the right, and midline y = 1.

The tangent function has a fundamentally different shape: it has vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ and repeats every π radians, not 2π. Understanding these graphing parameters is essential for modeling periodic phenomena like sound waves, tides, and seasonal temperature cycles.
steps: Identify the parent function (sine, cosine, or tangent) from the equation
Determine the amplitude |A| from the coefficient of the trig function
Calculate the period as 2π / |B| (or π / |B| for tangent)
Find the phase shift C by solving B(x − C) = 0 for x
Plot the midline y = D, mark the amplitude range, and sketch one full period

examples.title: Graphing a Transformed Sine Function
examples.text:
Describe the graph of y = 2 sin(x − π/4) + 3.

Step 1: Amplitude = |2| = 2.
Step 2: B = 1, so period = 2π/1 = 2π.
Step 3: Phase shift = π/4 to the right.
Step 4: Midline = y = 3.

The graph oscillates between y = 1 and y = 5, centered on y = 3, shifted right by π/4, with a standard period of 2π.

examples.title: Writing an Equation from Key Features
examples.text:
A cosine function has amplitude 4, period 3π, no phase shift, and midline y = −2. Write its equation.

Step 1: Amplitude → A = 4, so use 4·cos.
Step 2: Period = 2π/B = 3π → B = 2/3.
Step 3: No phase shift → C = 0.
Step 4: Midline → D = −2.

Equation: y = 4·cos((2/3)x) − 2.

lessons.tip: When identifying A, B, C, D from an equation, always factor B out of the parentheses first. For y = sin(2x − π), rewrite as y = sin(2(x − π/2)) so you can read the phase shift directly as π/2.

quiz.q: What is the period of y = 3 cos(4x)?
quiz.explanation: Period = 2π/|B| = 2π/4 = π/2.

quiz.q: What is the amplitude of y = −5 sin(x) + 1?
quiz.explanation: Amplitude = |A| = |−5| = 5. The negative sign reflects the graph but does not change the amplitude.

quiz.q: The phase shift of y = cos(x + π/3) is:
quiz.explanation: Rewrite as cos(x − (−π/3)): phase shift is −π/3, meaning π/3 to the left.

quiz.q: The midline of y = 2 sin(3x) − 4 is:
quiz.explanation: The vertical shift D = −4, so the midline is y = −4.

lessons.title: Probability Distributions
lessons.description: Create and interpret probability distributions for discrete random variables and calculate expected values.
lessons.formula:
E(X) = μ = Σ xᵢ·P(xᵢ)
Var(X) = Σ(xᵢ−μ)²·P(xᵢ)
σ = √Var(X)
All P(x): between 0 and 1, sum to 1
lessons.content: A probability distribution lists all values of a discrete random variable with their probabilities. The expected value E(X)=Σx·P(x) is the long-run average. The variance measures spread from the mean. All probabilities must be between 0 and 1 and sum to exactly 1. The expected value is not necessarily a value the variable can actually take.
steps: List all possible values with probabilities
Verify: all P(x) in [0,1] and sum to 1
Calculate E(X)=Σx·P(x)
Calculate variance: Σ(x−μ)²·P(x)
Standard deviation = √variance
lessons.tip: E(X) is the theoretical long-run average, NOT necessarily a value X can attain. For a fair die, E(X)=3.5 but you can never roll 3.5.

quiz.q: Valid distribution requires sum of all P(x) =
quiz.explanation: Probabilities must sum to exactly 1.

quiz.q: Expected value represents:
quiz.explanation: E(X) is the theoretical average over many trials.

quiz.q: If E(X)=4.2, which is true?
quiz.explanation: E(X) is what the average approaches over many repetitions.
